findings.title: Non-admin RCE via ERB execution of Table Manager definition files uploaded to targets_modified
findings.description:
##### Overview

`ConfigParser#parse_file` runs the configuration file through ERB (`run_erb` defaults to `true`), so any Ruby embedded in a parsed config file executes on the server. Table Manager parses definition files through this path: `Table.generate/load/binary/report/definition/save` → `TableManagerCore.*` → `TableConfig.process_file` → `ConfigParser.parse_file`. The definition file content is read via `TargetFile.body`, which reads from `#{scope}/targets_modified/#{name}`. A user who is **not** an admin (and does not hold `script_run`) can write an arbitrary file into `targets_modified` — the storage presigned-upload endpoint explicitly allows non-admins to write there, and it requires only `system_set` + `tlm` — and can then trigger Table Manager (which requires only `system`) to ERB-execute that file. The result is arbitrary Ruby code execution on the cmd-tlm-api server, a privilege escalation past the intended admin/`script_run` boundary for code execution.

##### Attack Path

```
attacker (system_set + tlm on a target) --POST /storage/upload/DEFAULT/targets_modified/INST/tables/config/evil_def.txt--> get_upload_presigned_request (targets_modified exempt from admin check) --presigned PUT--> object store now holds evil_def.txt containing <%= system("...") %>
attacker (system) --POST tables generate {definition: INST/tables/config/evil_def.txt}--> Table.generate --> get_definitions --> TargetFile.body reads scope/targets_modified/INST/tables/config/evil_def.txt --> TableManagerCore.generate --> TableConfig.process_file --> ConfigParser.parse_file(run_erb=true) --> ERB.new(...).result(binding) --> arbitrary Ruby executes on cmd-tlm-api server
```

The presigned upload handler gates non-`targets_modified`/`tmp` paths behind `admin`, but deliberately lets `system_set` users write into `targets_modified` (treated as "user modifications", presumed safe). Those same files are later interpreted as executable config: Table Manager reads the definition with `TargetFile.body` (which prefers `targets_modified`) and hands it to `ConfigParser.parse_file` with ERB enabled. Because Table Manager's read/generate actions require only `system`, no admin or script-execution permission is needed anywhere in the chain, so an operator-level account gains full server code execution. (`ScriptsController#create`, requiring only `script_edit`, is an alternative write vector into the same `targets_modified` location.)

##### Preconditions

- An Enterprise/RBAC deployment where permissions are distinct (in Core, a single password grants all permissions, so all authenticated users are already admin-equivalent and this is not an escalation).
- An authenticated attacker holding `system_set` and `tlm` (for the target directory) to upload via the presigned endpoint, plus `system` to invoke Table Manager — none of which is `admin` or `script_run`. A single operator account commonly holds all three. Alternatively `script_edit` can be used to write the file.
- The attacker chooses the definition filename, e.g. `INST/tables/config/evil_def.txt`; `..` is blocked by the sanitizer but is not needed since the write and read both target `targets_modified` under a normal path.
- Object-storage (bucket) mode or local mode — both are read by `TargetFile.body`.
findings.recommendation: Do not run ERB on Table Manager definition files that originate from user-writable locations (targets_modified). Either parse table definitions with run_erb disabled, or treat any file under targets_modified as untrusted data and refuse to ERB-evaluate it. More broadly, ensure that being able to write into targets_modified (system_set/script_edit) cannot yield server-side code execution: gate ConfigParser ERB rendering behind the same privilege required to install plugins/targets (admin), or sandbox/disable ERB for config parsed on behalf of non-admin requests. Reassess whether the storage presigned-upload exemption for targets_modified is safe given that those files are later interpreted as executable configuration.
findings.note:
ROOT CAUSE (config-overlay RCE). ConfigParser#parse_file defaults run_erb=true and evaluates file content as ERB Ruby: create_parsed_output_file -> ERB.new(File.read(filename)...).result(binding). TableConfig#process_file (table_config.rb:88) and PacketConfig/GenericConversion (cmd/tlm defs) both reach this on files pulled from the user-writable overlay via TargetFile.body -> {scope}/targets_modified/. VERIFIED CROSS-SCOPE CHAIN (auth non-admin -> RCE): (1) StorageController#get_upload_presigned_request guards on attacker-controlled params[:scope] and authorize_bucket_path downgrades to 'tlm' when a target is named + skips the admin check for targets_modified [sfind-ea3847c53c2e4c4494635775cab72237], letting a user with system_set in scope A + tlm on a target in scope B write {B}/targets_modified/TARGET/tables/*.txt; (2) TablesController#generate|save|save_as (guarded only by 'system' view perm) [sfind-2da48adb91f540c68e1ef958fe9cba57] -> Table.get_definitions -> TableManagerCore.process_file -> ConfigParser ERB -> arbitrary Ruby on the cmd-tlm-api server. Exploitability moderate (authenticated non-admin, no admin/script_run needed). Impact critical (server RCE on C2 ground software). Absorbs the generic_conversion eval facet (sfind-b199a0fc07dd48ff827d1ba644c85f0a, dismissed as duplicate). Matches published advisory GHSA-jjq7-m736-w977 (Critical).
  Related findings: sfind-ea3847c53c2e4c4494635775cab72237, sfind-2da48adb91f540c68e1ef958fe9cba57

findings.title: ButtonWidget eval()s button code from stored telemetry-screen definitions
findings.description:
##### Overview
The telemetry-screen `BUTTON` widget executes its second parameter (`this.parameters[1]`) as JavaScript in the operator's browser via `eval()`. The code string comes from the screen definition (operator/plugin-authored configuration). Anyone who can author or modify a screen definition that another user opens can run arbitrary JavaScript in that user's authenticated browser session (stored XSS / client-side code execution). This is the documented COSMOS button design, so it is only a security boundary issue when screen-authoring privilege is lower than the privilege of the operators who view the screen.

##### Attack Path
```
screen definition (BUTTON "text" "<js>") --stored config--> parameters[1] --> onClick(): eval(line) --runs in victim browser--> arbitrary JS with victim's session
```
The `onClick` handler splits `this.eval` (= `parameters[1]`) on `;;` and calls `eval(lines[i].trim())` for each fragment, awaiting any returned Promise. `parameters` is a Vue prop populated from the screen definition text. A malicious button body therefore executes with full access to the viewing operator's DOM, `localStorage.openc3Token`, and the COSMOS API client (`this.api`), enabling session/token theft or actions performed as the victim. `sendHazardousCmd` performs the same `eval` on `this.lastCmd`.

##### Preconditions
- A multi-user deployment where an attacker can create/modify a screen definition (e.g. via the screen editor or by loading a plugin/target) that is then opened by a higher-privileged operator.
- Victim opens the screen and clicks (or is enticed to click) the crafted button.
- Not exploitable as privilege escalation in COSMOS Core (no per-user RBAC); relevant in Enterprise / multi-tenant where screen-editing rights differ from viewing rights.
findings.recommendation: Avoid eval() of stored configuration. Prefer a constrained command/DSL (parse BUTTON bodies into a small set of allowed operations such as cmd()/run_script()) rather than executing arbitrary JS. If free-form JS must remain, gate screen creation/editing behind a privilege at least as high as any operator who can view the screen, and document the trust boundary. Ensure the auth token is not readable from JS (httpOnly cookie) so a compromised button cannot exfiltrate it.
findings.note: Stored, cross-user XSS/JS execution via Telemetry screen BUTTON widget. Stored button definitions reach eval() in ButtonWidget.vue, so a lower-privileged screen author can run arbitrary JavaScript in a higher-privileged operator's authenticated browser when they open the screen (screens are shared across operators). Exploitability moderate (needs screen-authoring access + victim opens screen); impact high (acts as the victim operator, can drive commands). Matches published advisory GHSA-gvf2-2rh5-mpgf (High).

findings.title: OS command injection via pypi_url interpolated into backtick pipinstall
findings.description:
##### Overview
During plugin install (`install_phase2`), when the plugin contains `pyproject.toml` or `requirements.txt`, the code builds a shell command string that interpolates the `pypi_url` setting and runs it with backticks (`/openc3/bin/pipinstall #{pip_args}`). `pypi_url` comes from the `pypi_url` scope setting (or the `PYPI_URL` env fallback). Because the value is placed into a shell command without escaping, shell metacharacters in the setting (`;`, `$( )`, backticks, `|`, `&`) are interpreted by the shell, yielding arbitrary command execution as the API/worker process. Note that the sibling `PythonPackageModel.put` builds the same pip invocation as an argv **array** (no shell), so this backtick form is an inconsistent and unsafe variant.

##### Attack Path
```
admin sets pypi_url setting (e.g. "https://x/$(malicious)") --> get_setting('pypi_url') --> pip_args = "-i #{pypi_url} #{gem_path}" --> `/openc3/bin/pipinstall #{pip_args}` (shell) --> injected command runs on server
```
The `pypi_url` setting is read at install time, `'/simple'` is appended, and it is concatenated into `pip_args`, which is then executed via backticks — a shell context. Any shell metacharacters in `pypi_url` execute. The value is admin-controlled (see preconditions), so in COSMOS Core this does not grant capability beyond what the admin already has (plugin.txt ERB already executes arbitrary Ruby on install); it is reported because a stored configuration value should never reach a shell, and the injection would become directly exploitable under any future privilege separation or additional write path to the setting.

##### Preconditions
- Attacker can set the `pypi_url` setting. Today this requires `admin` (settings API `set_setting` calls `authorize(permission: 'admin')`; scope seeding and local-mode sync are also admin/operator paths). No lower-privileged write path to `pypi_url` was found in this batch.
- A plugin containing `pyproject.toml` or `requirements.txt` is installed (admin plugin install), reaching `install_phase2`.
- `PIP_ENABLE_TRUSTED_HOST` unset or set — both branches interpolate `pypi_url` into the shell string.
findings.recommendation: Do not invoke pipinstall through a shell with an interpolated string. Use an argv array via ProcessManager.spawn / a non-shell exec (matching PythonPackageModel.put), e.g. run ["/openc3/bin/pipinstall", "-i", pypi_url, gem_path]. Additionally validate that pypi_url is a well-formed http(s) URL before use.
findings.note: OS command injection via the pypi_url setting. plugin_model.rb interpolates the admin-controlled pypi_url into a shell command string for pip install, allowing arbitrary command execution on the server. Exploitability difficult (admin-only, and admin already has plugin-install RCE reach) but profile marks OS command injection from any setting as always critical/high. Fix: pass argv array, never a shell string. Matches published advisory GHSA-vp3w-52v9-q57f (High).

findings.title: RunningScriptChannel replays any script id across scopes without ownership check (cross-tenant disclosure)
findings.description:
##### Overview
Subscribing to `RunningScriptChannel` streams a running script's full replay (backlog + live) selected purely by the client-supplied `params[:id]`. The subscription's auth check (`authenticate_subscription!`) only authorizes `script_view` for the connection's own `scope`; it never verifies that the requested running-script `id` belongs to that scope. Running-script ids are a single **global** monotonic counter (`OpenC3::Store.incr('running-script-id')`) and the replay stream key (`running-script-channel:<id>:replay`) is **not** scope-namespaced. An authenticated user with `script_view` in any one scope can therefore enumerate ids and receive the output, state, prompts, and full source code of scripts running in other scopes/tenants. The REST controllers enforce the id-to-scope binding (`ScriptStatusModel.get(name: params[:id], scope: params[:scope])`), but the WebSocket channel does not — a parallel-structure inconsistency.

##### Attack Path
```
attacker (script_view in scope A) --WS subscribe RunningScriptChannel {id: N}--> authenticate_subscription! authorizes only scope A --> subscribed() reads running-script-channel:N:replay (N = global id belonging to scope B) --transmit()/replay thread--> attacker receives scope B script output + source code
```
The connection authorizes `connection.scope` (attacker-chosen, their own scope). `subscribed` then builds `topic = "running-script-channel:#{params[:id]}:replay"` and both `Topic.xrange(topic)` (backlog, transmitted directly) and `RunningScriptReplayThread` (live tail) operate on that key with no scope filter. Because ids are globally sequential and the Redis stream key omits scope, the attacker guesses ids trivially. The running script broadcasts `{type: :file, text: @body.to_utf8}` (full source) and `{type: :output, line: ...}` (all output) onto that stream, so the attacker obtains another tenant's script source and runtime data.

##### Preconditions
- Multi-scope deployment where `scope` is an access-control boundary (COSMOS Enterprise / multi-tenant). In Core there is no per-scope RBAC so a valid token already grants all scopes and the gap is latent.
- Attacker holds a valid session token with `script_view` in at least one scope (e.g. their own tenant) but not the victim scope.
- A target script is (or was, within the 24h replay TTL) running in the victim scope; attacker knows/guesses its global integer id (sequential, easily enumerated).
findings.recommendation: In RunningScriptChannel#subscribed, before streaming, resolve the script status for params[:id] scoped to connection.scope (e.g. OpenC3::ScriptStatusModel.get(name: params[:id], scope: connection.scope)) and reject the subscription if it is nil. Alternatively namespace the replay stream key by scope (e.g. 'running-script-channel:<scope>:<id>:replay') and only allow subscription to keys within the authenticated scope. Apply the same id-to-scope binding used by the REST controllers.
findings.note: Cross-scope script output/source disclosure via WebSocket. RunningScriptChannel#subscribed streams running-script-channel:#{params[:id]}:replay using the client-supplied script id; the before_subscribe auth callback authorizes only the connection's scope, not that the requested id belongs to it. Script ids are globally sequential, so an authenticated script_view user can enumerate ids and read other scopes' script output/state. Exploitability moderate (authenticated, id enumeration); impact high (cross-tenant data). new/unverified.

findings.title: Unauthenticated global session termination (logout) enables denial of service
findings.description:
##### Overview

The Core `UsersController#logout` action has no authorization guard and calls `OpenC3::AuthModel.logout`, which deletes the entire `OPENC3__SESSIONS` Redis hash — invalidating *every* active session for the whole COSMOS instance, not just the caller's. Any unauthenticated client that can reach `PUT`/`PATCH /openc3-api/users/logout/:user` can forcibly log out all operators, and by repeating the request keep them logged out, producing a sustained denial of service against the authenticated UI/API of a command-and-control system.

##### Attack Path

```
unauthenticated PUT /openc3-api/users/logout/anything
  --routes to--> UsersController#logout   (no authorization() call, no before_action)
  --calls--> OpenC3::AuthModel.logout
  --executes--> Store.del('OPENC3__SESSIONS')   # deletes ALL session tokens
  --leads to--> every operator's session invalidated (global forced logout / DoS)
```

The route maps PATCH/PUT to `users#logout`. When the Enterprise controller cannot be required (Core deployments), the fallback stub defines `logout()` with no `authorization()` call, and no global `before_action`/middleware enforces auth in the cmd-tlm-api app (only `plugin_store_controller` has an unrelated `before_action`). `AuthModel.logout` unconditionally deletes the shared `SESSIONS_KEY` hash that holds all issued session tokens, so the effect is global rather than scoped to the caller — the `:user` route parameter is ignored entirely. On their next request every operator gets a 401 and must re-authenticate; looping the request keeps the outage active.

##### Preconditions

- Core (non-Enterprise) deployment: the `openc3-enterprise/controllers/users_controller` require raises `LoadError`, so the Core fallback stub is active.
- Authentication enabled (`$openc3_authorize` set / a password configured) so that sessions exist to terminate; with auth disabled the effect is moot.
- Network reachability to `/openc3-api/users/logout/:user` (the standard Traefik-exposed API surface). No credentials, token, or CSRF value are required.
findings.recommendation: Require an authenticated session on logout (e.g. `return unless authorization('system')`) and terminate only the caller's own session token via `OpenC3::AuthModel.terminate(token)` (honoring the authenticated identity / `:user` param) instead of calling the global `AuthModel.logout`. Reserve instance-wide session termination for an explicit admin-only operation.
findings.note: Unauthenticated global session termination. Route PATCH/PUT /openc3-api/users/logout/:user -> UsersController#logout calls OpenC3::AuthModel.logout with no authorization; AuthModel.logout does Store.del(SESSIONS_KEY), deleting the entire OPENC3__SESSIONS hash and invalidating EVERY operator's session. Single unauthenticated request, repeatable -> denial of operator command-and-control. Exploitability trivial. Profile: unauthenticated session-termination is always critical/high. Matches published advisory GHSA-25rh-53rx-456q (High).

findings.title: Unauthenticated insecure deserialization of JSON-RPC body (create_additions: true)
findings.description:
##### Overview

The public JSON-RPC endpoint `POST /openc3-api/api` (routed to `ApiController#api`) reads the raw request body and hands it to `OpenC3::Cts.instance.json_drb.process_request`, which calls `JsonRpcRequest.from_json`. That method parses the fully attacker-controlled body with `JSON.parse(request_data, allow_nan: true, create_additions: true)`. `create_additions: true` tells Ruby's `json` gem to perform object reconstruction: for any JSON object containing a `"json_class"` key it resolves the named constant via `JSON.deep_const_get` (repeated `const_get`) and, if that class defines `json_create`, instantiates it from attacker data. This parse happens *before* the method whitelist check and before any token/authorization check, so an unauthenticated remote client controls the input to a deserialization sink. This is CWE-502 (Deserialization of Untrusted Data) — the exact anti-pattern Ruby's json documentation warns can lead to RCE or DoS when the loaded gem set contains a class with a dangerous `json_create`.

##### Attack Path

```
POST /openc3-api/api (no before_action auth) --body--> ApiController#api (api_controller.rb:31)
  --request_data--> handle_post --> JsonDRb#process_request (json_drb.rb:252)
  --> JsonRpcRequest.from_json --> JSON.parse(request_data, create_additions: true) (json_rpc.rb:283)
  --> deep_const_get(attacker class) + klass.json_create(attacker hash) --> object injection / potential RCE
```

The route `post "/api" => "api#api"` has no authorization `before_action`; `ApplicationController` performs authorization only via opt-in `authorization(permission)` calls inside individual actions, and `ApiController#api` makes none. Authorization in this design is enforced *inside* each RPC method (via the token injected into `keyword_params`), which runs only after `public_send` on line 261 — long after the parse. `process_request` parses (line 252) before it even evaluates the method whitelist (line 257), so neither the whitelist nor the in-method auth guards the parse. The parse therefore executes `deep_const_get`/`json_create` on attacker-chosen class names and values with no authentication.

##### Preconditions

- Network reachability of `POST /openc3-api/api` (exposed through the Traefik proxy on the normal web port); no valid token, session, or password required to reach the parse.
- For object *injection* / autoload side effects: none beyond reachability (any loaded constant can be resolved; under Rails/Zeitwerk `const_get` on an unloaded name can trigger autoloading).
- For full *RCE*: the deployed gem set must contain at least one already-loaded class defining a dangerous `json_create` method. Only `String` (via `json/add/string`) and `Float` (defined in `json_rpc.rb`) are confirmed loaded from the openc3 library itself; the complete Rails/gem closure was not enumerable by static review, so the RCE escalation is conditional and unconfirmed.
findings.recommendation: Parse the JSON-RPC request body with `create_additions: false` (the modern json default) and reconstruct only the specific wire types COSMOS actually needs (the `Float`/`String` `json_class` shims) explicitly and safely after parsing, rather than allowing arbitrary `json_class` object reconstruction. Do this before the whitelist/auth so untrusted input never drives constant resolution. Separately, harden `Exception.from_hash` to only resolve a fixed allowlist of known exception classes instead of arbitrary `const_get`, and avoid `instance_variable_set` from peer-supplied data.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-912d80caa1e749dea0b1111e0efbb4e9 (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Unauthenticated insecure deserialization of JSON-RPC request body via JSON.parse(create_additions: true)
findings.description:
##### Overview

The primary OpenC3 API endpoint (`POST /openc3-api/api`) reads the raw HTTP body and, before any authentication or method-whitelist check, parses it with `JSON.parse(request_data, allow_nan: true, create_additions: true)`. With `create_additions: true`, the JSON gem resolves the class named in any embedded `"json_class"` field via `deep_const_get` and invokes that class's `json_create` on attacker-supplied data. Because this runs on unauthenticated, remote input, an attacker drives Ruby constant resolution and object instantiation through the parser (CWE-502). Depending on which `json_create`-defining classes are loaded in the API process, impact ranges from object injection / constant-autoload probing / DoS up to remote code execution.

##### Attack Path

```
attacker POST /openc3-api/api (no auth) --raw body--> ApiController#api
  --> JsonDRb#process_request --> JsonRpcRequest.from_json
  --> JSON.parse(body, create_additions: true) --"json_class"--> deep_const_get + Klass.json_create(attacker hash)
  --> object injection / gadget instantiation (potential RCE)
```

`ApiController#api` has no `before_action` authentication; it forwards the raw body to `JsonDRb#process_request`, whose very first step is `JsonRpcRequest.from_json` (json_drb.rb:252) — executed *before* the method-whitelist check (json_drb.rb:257) and before the per-method `authorize`/token validation that happens inside the dispatched API method. Thus `create_additions:true` parses fully unauthenticated input. `create_additions` makes the parser look up the attacker-named class and call its `json_create`, turning attacker JSON into arbitrary Ruby objects for every gadget class loaded in the process.

##### Preconditions

- Network reach to the cmd-tlm-api `POST /openc3-api/api` endpoint (the main COSMOS API). Assumed exposure: remote, pre-authentication (the parse precedes any auth check).
- For escalation to RCE: a class defining a dangerous `json_create` (a deserialization gadget) must be loaded in the cmd-tlm-api Ruby process. This file loads `json/add/string` and defines `Float.json_create`; I could not statically enumerate every `json/add/*` gadget transitively loaded by the gem/Rails dependency set, so the RCE ceiling is unconfirmed. The unauthenticated deserialization of untrusted input is confirmed.
findings.recommendation: Parse untrusted request bodies with create_additions:false (the safe default) and rebuild only the expected JSON-RPC fields (jsonrpc, method, params, keyword_params, id) explicitly. If typed values like Float Infinity/NaN must be supported, handle them with an explicit allowlisted transform rather than create_additions. Do not use const_get-based Exception.from_hash on any data that could be attacker-influenced.
findings.note: Pre-auth unsafe deserialization. json_rpc.rb parses request bodies with JSON.parse(..., create_additions: true) before authentication, enabling JSON object-injection (CVE-2020-10663 class). Today only benign additions (Time/Struct-like) are reachable, so confirmed impact is bounded object injection; becomes RCE if any gadget-carrying class with a json_create is loaded. Exploitability trivial to reach (unauthenticated HTTP), but full RCE precondition (dangerous gadget) is NOT satisfied in this codebase -> not promoted to P0. Fix: create_additions:false / allowlist. Canonical for the JSON create_additions root cause; duplicates sfind-237d8c05fdd94da8b5b274a367710fa5, sfind-81a10bf9e8d9493cb6bed4097391b3fe, sfind-618429dfc1ad4480beee7967b39d3f58 dismissed. new/unverified (no matching advisory in profile list).

findings.title: script_edit-guarded create/body execute attacker-supplied suite code server-side via Script.process_suite
findings.description:
##### Overview

The `create` action of `ScriptsController` is guarded only by the `script_edit` permission, yet when the submitted script text matches the suite-class regex it calls `Script.process_suite(name, params[:text], ...)`. `process_suite` writes the attacker-controlled text to a temporary `.rb`/`.py` file and launches a child process (`run_suite_analysis.rb`/`.py`) whose only job is `require ARGV[1]` — i.e. it *executes* the file's top-level code on the script-runner server. Code execution is normally a `script_run`-class capability, so a principal holding only `script_edit` (in an Enterprise RBAC deployment that separates editing from running) obtains arbitrary server-side code execution — a guard weaker than the side effect. Impact is amplified because the child process is handed full COSMOS service API credentials (`OPENC3_API_PASSWORD = OPENC3_SERVICE_PASSWORD`), so the executed code can drive privileged COSMOS APIs (e.g. send commands to hardware). The same `process_suite` sink is also reachable from `body`/`show` under the even-weaker `script_view` permission, executing stored suite content.

##### Attack Path

```
POST /script-api/scripts/<TARGET>/<name>.rb  (auth: script_edit)
  --params[:text] = "class X < OpenC3::Suite\nend\nsystem('cmd')"-->
Script.create --> Script.process_suite(name, params[:text])
  --writes text to temp .rb/.py; exec gate passes (OPENC3_SERVICE_PASSWORD set)-->
ChildProcess: ruby run_suite_analysis.rb SCOPE <temp>  -->  require <temp>
  --top-level Ruby/Python runs with service credentials-->
RCE on script-runner container + privileged COSMOS API access
```

The `create` handler only calls `authorization('script_edit')` (line 85). When `params[:text]` matches `SUITE_REGEX`/`PYTHON_SUITE_REGEX` (line 93) it forwards the raw text to `Script.process_suite` (line 94). `process_suite` writes the bytes to a tempfile and builds a child process (script.rb lines 62-81); as long as the execution gate is satisfied (an offline token, or `OPENC3_SERVICE_PASSWORD` present — set by default in `.env`) it calls `process.start` instead of returning early (script.rb lines 109-119). The child, `run_suite_analysis.rb`, does `require ARGV[1]` (line 24), which executes every top-level statement in the attacker's file. Because `create` requires only `script_edit`, a user who is trusted to edit procedures but not to execute them crosses that boundary and runs code with service-level credentials.

##### Preconditions

- `$openc3_authorize` is enforced (true — set by `config/initializers/authorization.rb`), and the attacker holds a valid token with `script_edit` but NOT `script_run`. This separation is only meaningful in Enterprise granular-RBAC deployments; in Core, `authorize()` ignores the permission string, so any authenticated user already has full access and this is not an escalation.
- The submitted text contains a suite class declaration to pass `SUITE_REGEX`/`PYTHON_SUITE_REGEX` (trivial, e.g. `class X < OpenC3::Suite`).
- The `process_suite` execution gate is satisfied: the principal has a valid `offline_access_token`, OR `OPENC3_SERVICE_PASSWORD` is set in the script-runner environment (it is set by default in this repo's `.env`).
- Could not verify: whether a standard Enterprise deployment (a) provisions a real role that grants `script_edit` without `script_run`, and (b) sets `OPENC3_SERVICE_PASSWORD` in the script-runner container. These conditions determine real-world exploitability, hence low confidence.
findings.recommendation: Do not execute attacker-supplied suite content from edit/view endpoints. Either (a) gate any `process_suite` invocation that runs script content behind `script_run` (or a dedicated execute permission) rather than `script_edit`/`script_view`, or (b) enumerate suite/group/case structure via static parsing (AST/lexical inspection) instead of `require`-ing the file, so viewing/editing a suite never executes it. Also avoid handing full `OPENC3_SERVICE_PASSWORD` credentials to suite-analysis children triggered by lower-privileged users.
findings.note: Script-suite code execution bypassing the approval/lifecycle control. scripts_controller script_edit/script_view paths process suite content server-side (process_suite/run_suite_analysis) so suite Ruby runs outside the script-run approval flow, reachable by a non-admin with only script view/edit rights. Exploitability moderate (Enterprise role separation + service creds); impact critical (server RCE). Matches published advisory GHSA-hf9c-xwpr-cjvr (High).

findings.title: AllScriptsChannel streams a global cross-scope feed of script start/complete events
findings.description:
##### Overview
`AllScriptsChannel` subscribes every client to the single global stream `script-api:all-scripts-channel`, which carries script start/complete events from ALL scopes (each event includes the script `filename` and its `scope`). The subscription only authorizes `script_view` for the connection's own scope, so an authenticated user in one scope receives script filenames and scope names for scripts running in every other scope/tenant — a cross-tenant metadata disclosure.

##### Attack Path
```
any running script (scope B) --publish {type,:filename,:scope} to all-scripts-channel--> global stream script-api:all-scripts-channel
attacker (script_view in scope A) --WS subscribe AllScriptsChannel--> stream_from same global stream --> receives scope B filenames + scope names
```
Producers call `running_script_anycable_publish("all-scripts-channel", {type: :start, filename:, active_scripts:, scope:})` for every script regardless of scope; this publishes to the un-scoped stream `script-api:all-scripts-channel`. `AllScriptsChannel#subscribed` does `stream_from "script-api:all-scripts-channel"` after only authorizing `connection.scope`, so all subscribers see all scopes' events.

##### Preconditions
- Multi-scope / Enterprise deployment where scope is an access-control boundary (latent in Core).
- Attacker holds a valid token with `script_view` in at least one scope.
- Disclosure is limited to metadata: script filenames (which reveal target/procedure names), scope names, and active-script counts — not script output or source.
findings.recommendation: Namespace the all-scripts stream per scope (e.g. stream_from "script-api:#{connection.scope}:all-scripts-channel" and publish to the matching per-scope stream), or filter events by connection.scope before transmit. Do not broadcast one scope's script metadata to subscribers authorized only for a different scope.
findings.note: Cross-scope script metadata disclosure. all_scripts_channel streams a global script-metadata feed not filtered to the subscriber's scope, so an authenticated script_view user sees other scopes' script names/state. Exploitability moderate (authenticated); impact medium. Fix: scope-filter the stream. new/unverified.

findings.title: Bucket RBAC downgrades write permission to read-level 'tlm' for target paths (cross-scope config write/delete)
findings.description:
##### Overview

`StorageController#authorize_bucket_path` computes `effective_permission = target_name ? 'tlm' : permission`, discarding the caller-supplied `permission:` argument whenever a target name can be extracted from the bucket path. The write endpoints (`get_upload_presigned_request`, `delete_bucket_item`, `delete_bucket_directory`) all call it with `permission: 'system_set'`, but for any target-specific config path (`{SCOPE}/targets_modified/{TARGET}/...`) that write-level requirement is silently downgraded to the read-level `tlm` permission. Because the separate top-level `authorization('system_set')` guard is evaluated against the attacker-controlled `params[:scope]` (independent of the path's scope) and the admin check is skipped for `targets_modified`/`tmp`, an Enterprise user who is an operator (`system_set`) in one scope and merely a telemetry viewer (`tlm`) on a target in a different scope can upload/overwrite or delete that other scope's modified target configuration files, escalating read access to write and crossing a scope (tenant) boundary.

##### Attack Path

```
attacker (system_set in scope A, tlm on TARGET in scope B)
  --POST get_upload_presigned_request(scope=A, bucket=OPENC3_CONFIG_BUCKET, object_id="B/targets_modified/TARGET/x.rb")-->
  authorization('system_set') checks scope A --passes-->
  authorize_bucket_path(..., permission:'system_set') --target present, effective_permission forced to 'tlm'--> authorize(tlm, TARGET, scope=B) passes
  --admin check skipped (targets_modified)--> presigned PUT URL for scope B returned
  --leads to--> cross-scope overwrite/delete of B's target config (definitions/screens/scripts)
```

The top-level `authorization('system_set')` only proves the attacker has write rights somewhere they chose (`params[:scope]`), not in the scope actually being written. `authorize_bucket_path` is the only check bound to the path's scope, and its permission gets replaced by `tlm` as soon as a target directory is present, so the write is authorized with a read permission. For `OPENC3_CONFIG_BUCKET` `targets_modified`/`tmp` the additional `authorization('admin')` gate is intentionally skipped, so nothing else re-imposes a write-level check. `delete_bucket_item`/`delete_bucket_directory` follow the same pattern, allowing deletion of another scope's target config.

##### Preconditions

- Deployment is OpenC3 Enterprise (the `openc3-enterprise` authorization gem is loaded so `permission`/`target_name`/`scope` are actually enforced; in Core `authorize` ignores them and every authenticated user already has full access).
- Attacker holds a role granting `system_set` in at least one scope A (their own operator scope) — used only to pass the top-level guard via `params[:scope]=A`.
- Attacker holds `tlm` (telemetry viewer) on the specific target TARGET in the victim scope B.
- Target path is `{B}/targets_modified/{TARGET}/...` (or `tmp`) in `OPENC3_CONFIG_BUCKET`, so the admin gate is skipped.
findings.recommendation: Do not discard the caller-supplied permission for target-specific paths. Use the stricter of the two (e.g. keep `permission` when it is `system_set`/`admin`, only using `tlm` as a baseline for read operations), and additionally require that the path's scope matches (or is independently authorized at the write level against) the scope used for the top-level guard. For write/delete flows, always authorize the write permission (`system_set`) against the path's actual scope+target before issuing a presigned PUT or deleting objects.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-ea3847c53c2e4c4494635775cab72237 (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Cross-scope config write/delete: top-level guard checks attacker-controlled params[:scope] while per-object check downgrades target paths to 'tlm'
findings.description:
##### Overview

Storage write/delete actions enforce authorization in two independent places that use two different scopes. The top-level `authorization('system_set'|'admin')` guard is evaluated against `params[:scope]` (fully attacker-controlled and unrelated to the object being written), while the only per-object scope enforcement — `authorize_bucket_path` — silently downgrades the required permission to `'tlm'` whenever a target name appears in the bucket key. For `targets_modified`/`tmp` keys the extra `admin` re-check is also skipped. Net effect in an Enterprise (multi-scope RBAC) deployment: a user who holds `system_set`/`admin` in *any one* scope of their own, plus mere `tlm` (telemetry-view) on a target in a *different* victim scope, can obtain upload presigned URLs for and delete objects under the victim scope's target config (`{VICTIM}/targets_modified/{TARGET}/...`, `{VICTIM}/targets/{TARGET}/...`, `{VICTIM}/target_archives/{TARGET}/...`). This is a cross-scope privilege escalation from read-only telemetry access to config write/delete.

##### Attack Path

```
attacker (system_set in own scope A + tlm on TARGET in victim scope B)
  --params[:scope]=A--> authorization('system_set') passes (checks scope A)
  --object_id=B/targets_modified/TARGET/evil--> authorize_bucket_path sees target TARGET, effective_permission='tlm'
  --tlm on TARGET in B passes--> targets_modified branch skips authorization('admin')
  --> presigned PUT / delete_object issued against victim scope B's target config
```

The request-level guard `authorization(permission)` in `ApplicationController` always uses `scope: params[:scope]` (application_controller.rb:54), so it never constrains which scope's objects are touched. The object's real scope is only checked by `authorize_bucket_path`, whose `effective_permission = target_name ? 'tlm' : permission` (storage_controller.rb:126) demotes every target-path write/delete to the `tlm` level. Because `params[:scope]` and the path scope are independent, the attacker satisfies the top guard with a scope they legitimately administer and directs the object operation at a different scope where they only hold `tlm`. For `targets_modified`/`tmp` keys the `key_split[1]` branch (storage_controller.rb:433-435, 635-637, 681-682) skips the `admin` re-check entirely, so `tlm` on the target is the whole control on the write/delete of executable-capable config (screens, procedures, cmd/tlm overrides, lib files).

##### Preconditions

- Enterprise deployment where `authorize()` performs real per-scope/per-target RBAC (Core returns `ANONYMOUS_USER`, so this is not exploitable in Core).
- Attacker holds `system_set` (for upload/`delete`) or `admin` (for deletes of `targets`/`target_archives`) in at least one scope they control, which they name in `params[:scope]`.
- Attacker holds `tlm` permission on the specific target in the victim scope (e.g. a cross-scope shared telemetry-view grant).
- Attacker knows the victim scope name and target name (both are enumerable/low-entropy).
findings.recommendation: Enforce authorization against the object's actual scope, not params[:scope]: derive the scope from the bucket key and pass it to a single authoritative check. Do not downgrade write/delete operations to 'tlm' — reserve the tlm baseline for read/list only, and require 'system_set' (writes) / 'admin' (deletes and non-targets_modified writes) against the path scope. Verify that params[:scope] equals the path scope, or drop the params[:scope]-based guard entirely in favor of the path-scoped check.
findings.note: Cross-scope config write/delete authorization bypass (Enterprise). storage_controller authorize_bucket_path sets effective_permission='tlm' when a target is named and skips the admin check for OPENC3_CONFIG_BUCKET targets_modified/tmp; the top guard checks the attacker-supplied params[:scope]. A user with system_set in their own scope + tlm on a target can obtain presigned writes into another scope's targets_modified. Exploitability moderate; impact high. This is the FIRST LINK of the config-overlay RCE chain -> see sink sfind-d23bc3556af4468fbbe483141d58b15a. Duplicate sfind-45d8913369914f2c973b725607999ebb dismissed. new/unverified.

findings.title: Global (shared) auth rate-limit counter enables unauthenticated login-lockout DoS
findings.description:
##### Overview
The login/password endpoints use a single global Redis counter for failed authentication attempts rather than a per-caller (per-IP / per-account) counter. Once the counter crosses the threshold, *every* subsequent login and password-change request is rejected with HTTP 429 for all users. An unauthenticated remote attacker can deliberately submit a small burst of wrong passwords to trip this global counter and thereby lock every legitimate user out of logging in or changing their password.

##### Attack Path
```
anonymous POST /auth/verify (wrong password) x10 --incr--> openc3__auth_bad_attempts__user >= MAX_BAD_ATTEMPTS --> user_rate_limited? true for ALL callers --> every /auth/verify and /auth/set returns 429 --> nobody can log in / change password
```
The `verify` action calls `user_rate_limited?` which reads the single global key `USER_BAD_ATTEMPTS_KEY` and returns true when `count >= MAX_BAD_ATTEMPTS` (default 10). Because the key is not scoped to the requester, ten failed attempts from any single anonymous client set the lock for everyone. `record_user_bad_attempt` sets the key's TTL (`BAD_ATTEMPTS_WINDOW`, default 120s) only on the first increment, so the lockout persists for the whole window; the attacker re-arms it with another ~10 requests every 120s, sustaining an indefinite login/password-change outage at negligible cost. The same design applies to `verify_service` via `SERVICE_BAD_ATTEMPTS_KEY`.

##### Preconditions
- Network reachability to the unauthenticated `/auth/verify` (and/or `/auth/verify_service`, `/auth/set`) endpoints; no credentials required.
- Redis/EphemeralStore reachable (normal operating condition) so the counter actually increments.
- Impacts availability of new logins and password changes only; already-issued session tokens and running operations continue to function.
findings.recommendation: Rate-limit per source identity (e.g. client IP and/or targeted account) instead of a single global key, or switch to an exponential-backoff/penalty scheme that never fully blocks unrelated legitimate users. If a global safety cap is desired, keep it high and combine it with per-IP limits so one client cannot deny login to all users. Consider returning success/failure timing that does not let the attacker cheaply detect when the lock is active.
findings.note: Unauthenticated login-lockout DoS. auth_controller uses a single global failure counter for login/password verification, so an unauthenticated attacker can trip the shared rate limit and lock out ALL operators from logging in or changing passwords. Existing sessions unaffected -> availability impact medium. Exploitability trivial (unauthenticated). Fix: per-identity/per-IP counter. Canonical for the global auth-lockout root cause; duplicates sfind-ea295929a6c64fedb527f21d970e169a, sfind-a92167bebe3b425ebfc701707da80d84 dismissed. new/unverified.

findings.title: Global (shared) auth rate-limit counter enables unauthenticated login-lockout DoS
findings.description:
##### Overview
The login rate limiter keys its bad-attempt counter on two fixed, process-global Redis strings (`openc3__auth_bad_attempts__user` and `openc3__auth_bad_attempts__service`) with no per-IP, per-account, or per-session component. Because COSMOS Core has a single shared password, an unauthenticated remote attacker can deliberately submit `MAX_BAD_ATTEMPTS` (default 10) wrong passwords within the window (default 120s) to trip the shared counter, after which every subsequent `/openc3-api/auth/verify`, `/auth/verify_service`, and `/auth/set` request returns HTTP 429 for all users. The attacker can repeat this indefinitely to keep the single operator permanently locked out of new logins and password changes on a command-and-control system.

##### Attack Path
```
unauthenticated POST /openc3-api/auth/verify (x10 wrong passwords)
  --record_user_bad_attempt increments global key--> openc3__auth_bad_attempts__user >= 10
  --user_rate_limited? returns true for ALL callers--> every /auth/verify & /auth/set -> HTTP 429
  --attacker repeats each window--> operator cannot log in or change password (availability DoS)
```
The login endpoints are unauthenticated by design. `record_user_bad_attempt` calls `EphemeralStore.incr(USER_BAD_ATTEMPTS_KEY)` on the fixed constant key, and `user_rate_limited?` reads that same fixed key and compares to `MAX_BAD_ATTEMPTS`. Since the key is not derived from the caller's IP/identity, one attacker's failures rate-limit everyone. `EphemeralStore` is the shared Valkey/Redis store, so the counter is global across all API replicas. Already-established session tokens keep working, so the impact is limited to blocking new authentication (login + password rotation), which is still a meaningful availability impact during an incident.

##### Preconditions
- The COSMOS Core (non-Keycloak) password auth path is in use (no enterprise IdP wrapping these endpoints).
- Attacker can reach `/openc3-api/auth/verify` (or `/auth/set`) — i.e. the API is network-reachable, which it is for any operator-facing deployment.
- No external per-IP rate limiting is layered in front (traefik ships without it by default).
findings.recommendation: Scope the bad-attempt counter to the requester (e.g. include a hashed client IP / X-Forwarded-For validated against the trusted proxy, or a per-account identifier) so one attacker cannot lock out everyone, and/or switch from a hard block to progressive backoff. Consider excluding successful/known clients and applying a separate, higher global cap only as a secondary safety net. Ensure the counter cannot be trivially reset or amplified.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-eca2fa941b294d6793d58b836565a04c (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Login rate-limit uses a single global counter, enabling unauthenticated lockout DoS of all users
findings.description:
##### Overview

The auth controller throttles bad login attempts using two fixed, global Redis keys (`openc3__auth_bad_attempts__user` and `openc3__auth_bad_attempts__service`) that are not keyed by client IP, username, or session. Any unauthenticated client can push the shared counter past `MAX_BAD_ATTEMPTS` (default 10) within `BAD_ATTEMPTS_WINDOW` (default 120s) by sending wrong passwords, after which `verify` and `set` return HTTP 429 for every caller until the window TTL expires. An unauthenticated attacker can thereby deny login (and password change) to all legitimate operators of the command-and-control system, sustained indefinitely with roughly 10 requests per two minutes.

##### Attack Path

```
attacker --POST /auth/verify wrong password x10--> record_user_bad_attempt --incr--> global key openc3__auth_bad_attempts__user
  --> user_rate_limited? returns true for everyone --> /auth/verify and /auth/set return 429 to all users
```

The counter key is a constant shared by all clients. Once the count reaches the threshold, `user_rate_limited?` returns true regardless of who calls, so legitimate operators get 429 on `/auth/verify` (obtaining a session) and `/auth/set` (password change). The lock self-heals after the TTL set on the first bad attempt, but the attacker trivially re-triggers it, producing continuous denial of login. (Already-issued valid sessions keep working, since they authenticate through the API's authorize() path, not this controller.)

##### Preconditions

- Network reachability of the unauthenticated `POST /auth/verify` (and/or `/auth/verify_service`) endpoint. Assumed exposure: remote, unauthenticated — the login endpoint is pre-auth by design.
- Core (password) authentication mode with any finite `MAX_BAD_ATTEMPTS`/`BAD_ATTEMPTS_WINDOW` (defaults 10 / 120s).
findings.recommendation: Key the bad-attempt counter by client identity (source IP and/or attempted username) rather than one global key, so a single attacker cannot lock out everyone. Optionally keep a high global threshold purely to slow brute force, but throttle per client for the lockout decision, and consider exponential backoff per source.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-eca2fa941b294d6793d58b836565a04c (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Pre-auth JSON deserialization with create_additions:true on the JSON-RPC request body
findings.description:
##### Overview

The JSON-RPC request parser deserializes the raw, unauthenticated HTTP request body with `JSON.parse(request_data, allow_nan: true, create_additions: true)`. The `create_additions: true` option re-enables the JSON object-creation additions feature (the vulnerability class of CVE-2020-10663 / "Unsafe Object Creation"): a body containing `{"json_class":"SomeClass", ...}` makes the parser resolve `SomeClass` and invoke its `json_create` to build an instance. This happens inside `JsonRpcRequest.from_json`, which is the very first thing `JsonDRb#process_request` does — before the method allow/deny check and before any `authorize()` call — so it is reachable by a completely unauthenticated attacker who can send a POST to the cmd-tlm-api endpoint. In this codebase only `String` and `Float` define `json_create` (both benign), and `json/add/core` is never required, so a concrete high-impact gadget chain cannot be demonstrated from static analysis of this commit alone. The finding is the unsafe-deserialization anti-pattern being exposed on a pre-auth surface, which turns any loaded class with a dangerous `json_create` (from a future dependency, stdlib `json/add/core`, or a gadget another investigator/batch identifies) into remote object instantiation without authentication.

##### Attack Path

```
unauthenticated POST /openc3-api/api (raw body)
  --influences--> ApiController#api -> handle_post (no before_action auth)
  --calls--> JsonDRb#process_request
  --calls--> JsonRpcRequest.from_json(request_data, headers)
  --reaches--> JSON.parse(request_data, create_additions: true)   [PRE-AUTH]
  --for {"json_class":"X"}--> X.json_create(hash)   (arbitrary object instantiation)
  --leads to--> object instantiation side effects / gadget-dependent RCE
```

The Rails `ApiController#api` action reads `req.body.read` and passes it straight to `handle_post` → `JsonDRb#process_request` with no controller-level authentication (`ApplicationController` defines an `authorization`/`authorize` helper but registers no `before_action`; authorization is performed inside individual API methods, which run only after dispatch). `process_request` calls `JsonRpcRequest.from_json` at its first line, and `from_json` calls `JSON.parse(..., create_additions: true)` on the attacker's bytes. With additions enabled, the parser instantiates any loaded class named in a `json_class` key that responds to `json_create`. Today that set is limited to `String`/`Float`, so impact is currently bounded; but the dangerous parse executes before authentication, so the moment an exploitable `json_create` gadget is loadable in the process the result is unauthenticated remote object creation. A related but lower-reachability variant exists on the client/response side: `Exception.from_hash` (lines 173-192) resolves an arbitrary class via `const_get` and calls `.new(message)` + `instance_variable_set`, reached from `json_drb_object.rb:126` when a JSON-DRB client parses a server error response.

##### Preconditions

- Network access to the cmd-tlm-api JSON-RPC endpoint (`POST /openc3-api/api`). No credentials needed: the `JSON.parse(create_additions:true)` runs before `authorize()` and before the method allow/deny check.
- For impact beyond instantiating `String`/`Float`: a class exposing an exploitable `json_create` (or, for the response-side path, any class with a dangerous single-arg `.new`) must be loaded in the Rails process — e.g. via `require 'json/add/core'` or a third-party gem. Not present at commit 77acb91; this specific escalation is UNVERIFIED and is what caps the rating at MEDIUM / medium confidence.
- The response-side `Exception.from_hash` variant additionally requires the attacker to control the JSON-DRB response `error.data` (a malicious/impersonated server or MITM against a JSON-DRB client).
findings.recommendation: Parse the request body with create_additions disabled (the JSON default) — e.g. JSON.parse(request_data, allow_nan: true) — or restrict object creation to an explicit allowlist of safe classes. If special floats (Infinity/NaN) and binary strings must round-trip through params, reconstruct them explicitly after a plain parse rather than relying on global JSON additions. Apply the same treatment to the other create_additions:true parses of externally-influenced data (Redis/Store stream values, on-disk config in local_mode.rb, websocket messages). For the response-side path, replace Exception.from_hash's const_get with a fixed allowlist of expected exception classes.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-912d80caa1e749dea0b1111e0efbb4e9 (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Table config file write/delete guarded only by 'system' (view) permission
findings.description:
##### Overview

Every `TablesController` action — including the config-mutating `save`, `save_as`, `generate`, and `destroy` — is guarded only by `authorization('system')`. `system` is the baseline view permission used across the codebase for read-only listings (e.g. `index`, `show`, storage read endpoints). These actions write and delete files in the config bucket under `{scope}/targets_modified/...` (via `Table` -> `OpenC3::TargetFile.create`/`destroy`). The same `targets_modified` objects, when written or deleted through `StorageController`, require `system_set` (writes) or `admin` (deletes/non-targets_modified). Consequently, an Enterprise user with only `system` (view) permission in a scope can create, overwrite, and delete target configuration files in that scope — an intra-scope privilege escalation from view to config write/delete.

##### Attack Path

```
attacker (system/view perm in scope S) --POST /tables/*name or DELETE /tables/*name--> authorization('system') passes --> Table.save/generate/destroy --> TargetFile.create/destroy writes/deletes {S}/targets_modified/<name> in CONFIG bucket
```

`save`/`generate` write `.bin` content into `targets_modified`, and `destroy` deletes `{scope}/targets_modified/<name>` where `name` may contain `/` (allow_forward_slash), so a view-level user can delete arbitrary modified files (screens, procedures, cmd/tlm overrides) for any target in the scope. `save_as` copies a readable file to any name under `targets_modified`. The inconsistency with `StorageController` (which requires `system_set`/`admin` for the identical bucket region) demonstrates that `system` is weaker than the operation's side effect.

##### Preconditions

- Enterprise deployment with real per-scope RBAC where a role can hold `system` without `system_set`/`admin` (Core ignores permission strings).
- Attacker is authenticated and has `system` (view) permission in the target scope, which they supply as `params[:scope]`.
- A valid table/binary/definition path in that scope for the read-then-write actions; `destroy` needs only a known modified-file name.
findings.recommendation: Raise the guards on config-mutating table actions (save, save_as, generate, destroy) to 'system_set' (and 'admin' where consistent with StorageController deletes), matching the permission required to write/delete the same targets_modified objects elsewhere. Keep read actions (index, body, binary, definition, report, load) at 'system'.
findings.note: Table mutation/generation guarded only by read-level 'system'. tables_controller save/save_as/generate/destroy all use authorization('system') (a view-level permission), letting a low-privileged Enterprise user write/delete/generate target table config and definitions. Exploitability moderate; impact high (config integrity + it is the RCE TRIGGER that parses attacker overlay files through TableManager/ConfigParser ERB -> see sink sfind-d23bc3556af4468fbbe483141d58b15a). Duplicate sfind-c441a35cbc1c4395aa01be09f5d19f78 dismissed. new/unverified.

findings.title: Table write/delete/generate operations guarded only by read-level 'system' permission
findings.description:
##### Overview

Every `TablesController` action, including the mutating ones (`save`, `save_as`, `generate`, `destroy`, `lock`, `unlock`), is guarded only by `authorization('system')` — the read-level permission the same service uses for listing/reading. Every other CRUD controller in this service guards writes with a higher permission (`script_run` for trigger/reaction/notes/timeline writes, `system_set` for storage writes), and `StorageController` specifically requires `system_set` to upload or delete files in the very same `targets_modified` bucket area that `Table.save`/`create`/`destroy` write to. In an Enterprise deployment where `system` is granted to a read-only viewer role, this lets a viewer create, overwrite, regenerate, and delete target table binary/definition files — an authorization gap versus the write-level permission the equivalent storage endpoints demand.

##### Attack Path

```
attacker (only read-level 'system' on scope S)
  --POST tables/save (or destroy/generate/save_as) with scope=S-->
  authorization('system') --passes (read permission)-->
  Table.save/destroy/generate --> TargetFile.create/destroy writes/deletes {S}/targets_modified/... in OPENC3_CONFIG_BUCKET
  --leads to--> viewer modifies/deletes target table config that StorageController protects with 'system_set'
```

The controller never requires a write/`_set` permission for state-changing actions, so the check that succeeds (`system`) is weaker than the side effect (persisting or deleting bucket objects). The same objects, reached through `StorageController#get_upload_presigned_request`/`delete_bucket_item`, require `system_set`, demonstrating the intended write-permission level is higher than `system`.

##### Preconditions

- Deployment is OpenC3 Enterprise (permission strings are enforced; in Core they are ignored and any authenticated user already has full access).
- The Enterprise role→permission mapping grants `system` to a role that is not intended to have write access (e.g. a read-only viewer). This mapping lives in the external `openc3-enterprise` gem and could not be confirmed from this repository — the finding rests on the in-repo convention (all other writes use `script_run`/`system_set`; storage requires `system_set` for the same files).
- Attacker has `system` on the target scope passed as `params[:scope]`.
findings.recommendation: Raise the authorization level for state-changing table actions to a write permission consistent with the rest of the service — `system_set` (matching StorageController's guards on the same targets_modified files) for save/save_as/generate/destroy, keeping `system` only for read actions (index/binary/definition/report/body/load). Confirm against the Enterprise role→permission mapping that the chosen permission is not granted to read-only viewers.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-2da48adb91f540c68e1ef958fe9cba57 (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Unauthenticated cross-scope metrics disclosure (/openc3-api/internal/metrics has no authorization guard)
findings.description:
##### Overview

The `InternalMetricsController#index` action serves the Prometheus scrape endpoint at `/openc3-api/internal/metrics` and performs **no** authorization check (there is no `return unless authorization(...)` call, unlike the sibling `InternalHealthController#health` which requires `authorization('system')`). It enumerates *every* scope via `ScopeModel.names` and dumps all stored metrics for each scope. Traefik forwards `/openc3-api/*` straight to this API with no path filtering, so any remote, unauthenticated client can retrieve operational metrics for the entire deployment — request counters, per-target/per-microservice metric names, and label values (method/path/code) — which for a command-and-control system is useful reconnaissance about which targets exist and how they are being operated.

##### Attack Path

```
anonymous HTTP GET /openc3-api/internal/metrics --Traefik removeFirst--> /internal/metrics --route--> InternalMetricsController#index (no authorization() call) --ScopeModel.names + MetricModel.all(scope)--> cross-scope Prometheus metrics rendered to unauthenticated caller
```

The api-router in `traefik.yaml` matches `PathPrefix('/openc3-api')` (priority 8) and strips the prefix, so the internal endpoints are reachable from the same public entrypoint as the rest of the API with no separate network restriction. `routes.rb` maps `/internal/metrics` to `internal_metrics#index`. The action body never calls `authorization`, so even when a Core password (`$openc3_authorize`) is configured, this endpoint bypasses it. The loop iterates all scopes and returns metric names plus `k="v"` labels, disclosing operational structure across every scope.

##### Preconditions

- Network reachability to the COSMOS Traefik entrypoint (default port 2900), i.e. anyone who can reach the web UI.
- No authenticated session or token required — the action has no guard regardless of whether `$openc3_authorize` (Core password auth) is enabled.
- Metrics have been generated (normal operation), so the disclosed data reflects live target/microservice activity.
findings.recommendation: Add an authorization guard to `index` consistent with the other internal endpoints (e.g. `return unless authorization('system')`), or restrict `/internal/*` to an internal-only Traefik router / IP allowlist so the Prometheus scrape target is not reachable from the public entrypoint. If unauthenticated scraping is required, expose metrics only on an internal network interface.
findings.note: Unauthenticated metrics disclosure. GET /openc3-api/internal/metrics (internal_metrics_controller) has no authorization and exposes cross-scope operational/runtime metrics to any unauthenticated client. Exploitability trivial; impact medium (info disclosure / recon aid on C2 system). Fix: require authorization or restrict to the internal network. new/unverified.

findings.title: Unauthenticated disclosure of internal microservice topology via /openc3-api/traefik
findings.description:
##### Overview

The `traefik` action of `MicroservicesController` has no `authorization(...)` guard, unlike every other action in the controller (`index`, `create`, `show`, `update`, `destroy`, `start`, `stop`). It enumerates every microservice in the deployment across ALL scopes and returns a Traefik dynamic-config document that exposes each microservice's name, URL path prefix, backend port, shard, and the operator hostname. Because it is routed under the public `/openc3-api` PathPrefix with no auth middleware, any remote, unauthenticated attacker can retrieve a map of the system's internal service topology — even though the rest of the API requires a valid token in production (`$openc3_authorize = true`).

##### Attack Path

```
anonymous GET /openc3-api/traefik --routed by Traefik api-router (PathPrefix /openc3-api, no auth)--> MicroservicesController#traefik (no authorization guard) --MicroserviceModel.all (no scope)--> JSON with names/prefixes/ports/operator-hostname --leads to--> internal topology recon
```

Traefik's `api-router` (priority 8) forwards every `/openc3-api/*` request to the cmd-tlm-api service with no authentication middleware. In production, `config/initializers/cts.rb` includes `AuthorizedApi`, which sets `$openc3_authorize = true`, so guarded actions reject requests lacking a valid token. The `traefik` action, however, never calls `authorization(...)`, and there is no global `before_action` enforcing auth (confirmed across the controllers directory). It calls `OpenC3::MicroserviceModel.all` with no `scope:` argument, which returns microservices from every scope, then emits their `name`, `prefix`, `port`, and the `OPENC3_OPERATOR_HOSTNAME`. An attacker learns the internal service/tool inventory, path prefixes, ports, and hostnames of the command-and-control system without credentials.

##### Preconditions

- The cmd-tlm-api is reachable by the attacker at the public Traefik entrypoint (default `:2900`), i.e. any internet- or network-facing deployment.
- No credentials required: the action has no `authorization()` call and Traefik applies no auth middleware to `/openc3-api`.
- Response sensitivity depends on how descriptive the deployment's microservice names/prefixes are (they typically embed scope, type, and target/tool names).
findings.recommendation: Do not expose the Traefik provider endpoint on the public `/openc3-api` prefix. Either (a) restrict `/openc3-api/traefik` at the proxy so it is only reachable from the internal Docker/K8s network (e.g. a dedicated internal-only entrypoint/port that Traefik polls, excluded from the public router), or (b) add an authentication check to the action. Also scope `MicroserviceModel.all` appropriately rather than returning every scope, and avoid interpolating raw microservice `prefix` values into Traefik rule strings (line 85) to prevent rule/route manipulation by anyone who can create microservices.
findings.note: Unauthenticated microservice topology disclosure. GET /traefik (microservices_controller#traefik) is unauthenticated and reveals microservice routing/topology (and interpolates raw route prefixes). Exploitability trivial; impact medium (recon). Fix: authenticate or serve only to the proxy's internal network. new/unverified.

findings.title: Unbounded recurring-activity expansion enables memory/CPU denial of service
findings.description:
##### Overview

When a recurring activity is created, `ActivityModel#create` iterates from the activity start to the attacker-supplied `@recurring['end']` in steps derived from the attacker-supplied `@recurring['frequency']`/`@recurring['span']`, generating one activity record (and JSON blob) per step inside a single Redis `MULTI` pipeline. The per-occurrence duration is capped at `MAX_DURATION` (86400s) by `validate_input`, but neither the recurrence end time nor the total number of generated occurrences is bounded. An authenticated user can post a recurring activity with a far-future `end` and a small `frequency` (e.g. 1 minute), forcing the API worker to build hundreds of millions of records in memory and flood Redis — exhausting memory/CPU on the cmd-tlm-api worker and the Valkey store.

##### Attack Path

```
POST /activity (recurring: {end: far-future epoch, frequency: 1, span: 'minutes'}) --authorization('script_run')--> create_timeline_activity --_cal_to_epoch(end) has no upper bound--> ActivityModel#create --> (@start..@recurring['end']).step(recurrence).each { build JSON + multi.zadd } --> ~(end-start)/60 iterations --> OOM / Redis flood (DoS)
```

`ActivityController#create` permits `recurring` params and calls `create_timeline_activity`, which converts `recurring['end']` to an epoch integer with `_cal_to_epoch` (accepts a raw integer unchanged, no ceiling). `ActivityModel#create` computes `recurrence = frequency.to_i * multiplier` and loops `(@start..@recurring['end']).step(recurrence)`; `validate_input` at line 279 only checks the single occurrence's duration, not the recurrence horizon, so the iteration count is entirely attacker-controlled. Each iteration allocates a JSON document and buffers a `zadd` into the in-memory `Store.multi` block, so a large horizon translates directly into unbounded memory and Redis load.

##### Preconditions

- `$openc3_authorize` enabled and the attacker holds a token with the `script_run` permission (in COSMOS Core, the single shared password grants this).
- A timeline already exists in the scope (create raises otherwise); the attacker knows/uses its name.
- `recurring['end']`, `frequency`, and `span` are all present and valid enough that `recurrence > 0` (e.g. span='minutes', frequency>=1), and `end` is set far in the future.
findings.recommendation: Bound recurring activities: reject a recurrence horizon beyond a sane maximum (e.g. cap end - start, or cap the total number of generated occurrences), enforce a minimum recurrence step, and validate frequency is a positive integer. Consider generating occurrences lazily instead of materializing every occurrence into a single Redis MULTI.
findings.note: Resource-exhaustion DoS. activity_model.rb materializes recurring activities without an effective bound, so an authenticated user creating a wide/long recurrence can exhaust memory/CPU/storage. Exploitability moderate (authenticated); impact medium (availability). Fix: cap horizon/count. new/unverified.

findings.title: Unrestricted raw Redis command dispatch via /redis/exec (scope-isolation bypass in multi-tenant)
findings.description:
##### Overview
The `RedisController#execute_raw` action (`POST /redis/exec`) reads the raw request body, takes the first whitespace-delimited token as a Redis command, and dispatches it via `public_send` to the shared `OpenC3::Store`/`EphemeralStore` connection. The only restriction is a one-element denylist (`AUTH`); there is no command allowlist. Because the command is upcased before dispatch, only Redis command forwarding (via `Store#method_missing`) is reachable and no Ruby-level method (`send`, `eval`, etc.) can be invoked, so this is not RCE. However, the endpoint lets any caller who passes the `admin` guard run *arbitrary* Redis commands against the shared data store, including destructive ones (`FLUSHALL`, `CONFIG SET`) and cross-scope reads/writes (`KEYS *`, `GET OTHERSCOPE__...`). In COSMOS Enterprise, the `admin` permission is scope-level, so a tenant/scope admin can read and modify data belonging to every other scope, bypassing scope isolation. In Core (single shared role) this grants nothing beyond what an authenticated admin already has.

##### Attack Path
```
POST /redis/exec (scope=A, admin token for scope A) --body "KEYS *" / "GET B__secret" / "FLUSHALL"--> command=args[0].upcase (only 'AUTH' denied) --> Store.instance(db_shard).public_send(command, args[1..-1]) --method_missing--> redis.public_send(command, ...) --> reads/wipes ALL scopes' Redis data
```
The `authorization('admin')` guard checks the caller's `admin` permission for `params[:scope]` (scope A). The subsequently executed Redis command, however, operates on the entire Redis DB shard, whose keys are namespaced per scope but are not otherwise isolated. Nothing constrains the command to scope A's key prefix, so a scope-A admin can enumerate and manipulate other scopes' keys, or issue server-wide destructive commands.

##### Preconditions
- Deployment with `$openc3_authorize = true` (set at boot by `Cts`/`AuthorizedApi`).
- Attacker holds a valid token that satisfies the `admin` permission for at least one scope (in Enterprise, a scope-level admin account; in Core, any authenticated user).
- Impact beyond the attacker's own scope is only meaningful in a multi-tenant (Enterprise, multi-scope) deployment; in single-tenant Core there is no privilege boundary crossed.
- Note: this appears to be an intended admin debugging tool in stock OpenC3; flagged for the missing command allowlist / scope-isolation gap rather than a coding defect.
findings.recommendation: Replace the AUTH-only denylist with a strict allowlist of the specific read-only/diagnostic Redis commands the UI actually needs, and reject everything else. Constrain any key arguments to the caller's authorized scope prefix (e.g. require and prepend `params[:scope] + '__'`), or require `superadmin` for this endpoint if global raw access is truly needed. Also handle an empty body (args[0] may be nil → NoMethodError).
findings.note: Raw Redis command dispatch. redis_controller forwards commands via public_send to the Valkey store with only an AUTH denylist; because commands are upcased, only Redis command forwarding (not Ruby methods like send/eval) is reachable, so this is data-plane access, not code execution. Still allows a scope admin cross-scope read/write/wipe of shared Valkey state. Intended admin/debug tool -> exploitability difficult (scope admin); impact high (tenant boundary). Defense-in-depth: scope-key allowlist. new/unverified. (Note: the profile's GHSA-q2gf-g584-w94p concerns a JsonDRb public_send denylist bypass, a different sink; not asserted here.)

findings.title: Unsafe JSON deserialization (create_additions: true) of attacker-influenced interface command topic data
findings.description:
##### Overview

The interface/router command handler threads parse every field of the messages they consume from the Redis command topics with `JSON.parse(..., allow_nan: true, create_additions: true)`. `create_additions: true` makes the Ruby `json` gem honor a `json_class` directive inside the JSON: for `{"json_class":"SomeClass",...}` it resolves the named constant and calls `SomeClass.json_create(hash)`, instantiating an arbitrary loaded Ruby object from attacker-influenced data. The `params`/`cmd_params` etc. written to these topics originate from the authenticated API caller and are re-serialized with `JSON.generate`, so an attacker who can enqueue an interface command (connect, interface_cmd, protocol_cmd, target_control, or a raw command) can smuggle a `json_class` key that survives the round-trip and is honored on the consumer side. This is object injection / unsafe deserialization; whether it reaches full RCE depends on the `json_create` gadgets loaded in the operator process (no core-defined RCE gadget was confirmed in this batch).

##### Attack Path

```
authenticated user --connect/cmd API with crafted params hash--> InterfaceTopic.connect_interface --JSON.generate(interface_params)--> Redis {scope__CMD}INTERFACE__name topic --> InterfaceCmdHandlerThread#run --JSON.parse(msg_hash['params'], create_additions: true)--> Class.json_create(attacker hash) --> arbitrary object instantiation
```

The API side (`InterfaceTopic.connect_interface`, line 107) serializes the caller-supplied `interface_params` array verbatim with `JSON.generate`; a nested hash containing `"json_class"` is preserved faithfully. The consumer (`interface_microservice.rb` line 116, and siblings at 159, 171, 203, 241, 436, 457, 469) parses that string with `create_additions: true`, so the gem resolves the attacker-named constant and invokes its `json_create`. Because there is no allow-list on the class name, any loaded class defining `json_create` can be instantiated with attacker-chosen fields.

##### Preconditions

- `$openc3_authorize` is enabled and the attacker holds a valid token/password with command authorization for at least one interface/router (in COSMOS Core this is a single shared password).
- The attacker can invoke an interface/router action that round-trips a hash they control (connect `params`, `interface_cmd`, `protocol_cmd`, `target_control`, or `cmd_params`).
- Reaching code execution (vs. mere object injection) additionally requires a class with a dangerous `json_create` to be loaded in the operator process; no such gadget was confirmed within this batch.
findings.recommendation: Parse these topic fields with create_additions disabled (the Ruby json default), e.g. `JSON.parse(str, allow_nan: true)` without create_additions, or restrict deserialization to an explicit allow-list of expected classes. If object round-tripping is genuinely required, replace it with an explicit schema/constructor rather than relying on json_class directives from untrusted data.
findings.note: Unsafe deserialization on interface data. interface_microservice.rb uses JSON.parse(..., allow_nan:true, create_additions:true) on attacker-influenced interface command data. Requires a command-authorized user and a Redis round-trip, and no dangerous json_create gadget is currently loaded -> object injection only. Exploitability difficult; impact medium. Fix: create_additions:false. new/unverified.

findings.title: Admin-configurable pypi_url used unvalidated as pip index (SSRF / supply-chain sink)
findings.description:
##### Overview

`PythonPackageModel.install` reads the `pypi_url` setting and passes it verbatim to `pip` as the package index (`-i <pypi_url>`, and as `--trusted-host URI.parse(pypi_url).host`). The value is never validated for scheme/host, so whoever controls the `pypi_url` setting can force the server to make outbound requests to an arbitrary host (SSRF into the cluster / cloud metadata) and/or point pip at a malicious index to poison the packages that get installed and executed (supply-chain). In isolation this is gated: both writing the setting (`set_setting`) and triggering an install (`PackagesController#create`, plugin install) require the `admin` permission, and an admin already has code-execution-equivalent capability via plugin/package upload. It is reported at LOW as a defense-in-depth gap and, more importantly, as a chain handoff: if any other defect lets a lower-privileged actor set `pypi_url` or reach `install`, this sink turns a setting write into server-side SSRF + arbitrary code execution.

##### Attack Path

```
set pypi_url setting (admin) --stored in Redis--> get_setting('pypi_url') [L73] --unvalidated--> pip_args ['-i', pypi_url, '--trusted-host', URI.parse(pypi_url).host] [L93] --spawn pipinstall [L95]--> outbound HTTP to attacker host + install packages from attacker index --> SSRF + supply-chain RCE
```

The `pypi_url` setting is fetched at line 73 and, with no scheme/host allowlist, becomes pip's index URL and trusted host at lines 91/93. `ProcessManager.spawn` (line 95) then runs `/openc3/bin/pipinstall` with those args, so pip contacts the attacker-specified host to resolve/download dependencies, which are then installed (native code execution) under the service identity. Pointing the host at an internal service or `169.254.169.254` yields SSRF; pointing it at a hostile mirror yields dependency poisoning.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker can write the `pypi_url` setting, which requires the `admin` permission (`set_setting` calls `authorize(permission: 'admin')`). In COSMOS Core all authenticated users share one password and are effectively admin; in Enterprise this requires the admin role.
- A package install is triggered (admin uploads a package via `PackagesController#create`, or a plugin install runs), which calls `PythonPackageModel.install`.
- For metadata/internal SSRF impact, an internal HTTP target (e.g. cloud metadata endpoint) must be reachable from the process container. The response is not returned to the attacker (blind SSRF) unless leaked via pip error output.
