- Marginal in isolation because an admin already has plugin-install RCE; severity rises to HIGH/CRITICAL only if composed with a separate bug that lets a non-admin set the setting or reach `install`.
findings.recommendation: Validate `pypi_url` before use: require an https:// (or explicitly allowed) scheme, resolve and reject private/link-local/metadata IP ranges (e.g. 127.0.0.0/8, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 169.254.0.0/16), and ideally constrain to an operator-provided allowlist of mirror hosts. Apply the same validation in `set_setting` when the setting name is `pypi_url`/`rubygems_url` so bad values are rejected at write time. Avoid `--trusted-host` on untrusted hosts.
findings.note: Admin-controlled pypi_url passed to pip as index/trusted-host -> SSRF / supply-chain risk. Admin-gated, and distinct from the pypi_url OS command injection (sfind-c4f38280a31448f99494929bd380b39d). Exploitability difficult (admin); impact low. Fix: validate/allowlist the index URL. new/unverified.

findings.title: Config-derived Ruby eval in GenericConversion (intentional RCE sink, auth-gated)
findings.description:
##### Overview

`GenericConversion#call` runs `eval(@code_to_eval)` where `@code_to_eval` is a Ruby source string taken verbatim from a target's packet-definition config (`GENERIC_READ_CONVERSION_START/END` and `GENERIC_WRITE_CONVERSION_START/END` blocks). When a packet/item that carries such a conversion is processed, the string executes as Ruby on the COSMOS server, i.e. OS-level code execution inside the container. The evaluated string is *not* derived from runtime telemetry/command values (those are only referenced as local variables `value`/`packet`/`buffer` — data, not code); its sole source is config authored at plugin/target install time or via target-file edits. Authoring/editing that config is gated behind authentication — in COSMOS Core a single shared password grants all permissions (`authorize` ignores the `permission` argument), and such an operator already has equivalent arbitrary code execution via Script Runner; in Enterprise it is behind `system_set`/`admin` RBAC. No path in this file lets lower-privileged or unauthenticated input set the code. It is reported at LOW as a precise chain endpoint: any *separate* bug that permits writing/altering a target's config files (path traversal, missing-auth write to the config bucket, etc.) would compose with this sink to yield RCE.

##### Attack Path

```
target config .txt (GENERIC_*_CONVERSION block) --parsed by--> PacketConfig#process_file --GenericConversion.new(@proc_text)--> item.read/write_conversion --packet processed--> GenericConversion#call --eval(@code_to_eval)--> Ruby/OS code execution on server
```

`PacketConfig#process_file` accumulates the lines between `GENERIC_*_CONVERSION_START` and `_END` into `@proc_text` and constructs a `GenericConversion` with it. On each packet read/write, the conversion's `call` method evaluates that text. The only injection vector is the config text itself, so whoever can author or modify a target's packet definition can execute arbitrary Ruby once the packet is processed.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker can create or modify a target's packet-definition config (install a plugin/target, or write to the target config storage bucket). In COSMOS Core any authenticated user (shared password) can do this and already holds equivalent code-exec via Script Runner; a lower-privilege or unauthenticated config-write path found elsewhere would make this an escalation to RCE.
- A packet/item using the crafted conversion is subsequently processed (telemetry received or command built).
findings.recommendation: This eval is intentional COSMOS behavior, so the priority is protecting the authoring path: ensure every config-authoring endpoint (plugin install, target file writes to the config bucket, screen/target file edits) enforces strong authorization in Enterprise and is network-restricted/trusted-operator-only in Core, and treat any new file-write path into target config as RCE-equivalent. Longer term, consider offering non-eval conversion primitives or sandboxing conversion evaluation.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-d23bc3556af4468fbbe483141d58b15a (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Core session tokens never expire; stale per-process cache delays termination
findings.description:
##### Overview

WebSocket connection and channel authentication funnel through `OpenC3::Authorization#authorize` → `AuthModel.verify` → `verify_no_service`. In COSMOS Core, a session token's only validity requirement is membership in the Redis hash `OPENC3__SESSIONS`. `generate_session` stores `Time.now.iso8601` as the hash value, but no code ever reads that timestamp to enforce an expiry, and no TTL/pruning is applied to the key. Consequently a session token is valid indefinitely once issued — there is no idle timeout or absolute lifetime (CWE-613, Insufficient Session Expiration). Additionally, `verify_no_service` serves validity from a process-local class-variable cache (`@@session_cache`) for up to 5 minutes without re-reading Redis, so a token revoked via `terminate`/`logout` on one worker can continue to authenticate on other worker processes/containers until their caches age out.

##### Attack Path

```
attacker obtains a valid session token (log leak / browser storage / shoulder-surf)
  --> token stays in OPENC3__SESSIONS forever (no expiry read of the stored timestamp)
  --> authorize()/AuthModel.verify keeps returning true across connection.rb + channel.rb auth
  --> indefinite unauthorized access; even after logout, stale @@session_cache validates it for up to 5 min on other workers
```

The connection auth path (`connection.rb:44-55`) and the channel subscription path both call `authorize(... token: ...)`, which for Core reduces to `AuthModel.verify(token)`. Because verification is pure set-membership with no time check, token lifetime is unbounded, amplifying the impact of any token disclosure.

##### Preconditions

- The attacker must obtain a previously issued, valid session token (this finding concerns lifetime/revocation, not initial token theft).
- COSMOS Core auth mode (opaque Redis session tokens). Enterprise/Keycloak token expiry is handled separately and is out of scope for this path.
- For the revocation-latency variant: a multi-process/multi-container deployment where `terminate`/`logout` runs on a different process than the one still serving the token.
findings.recommendation: Enforce session expiration: store an expiry (or read the existing iso8601 timestamp) and reject tokens older than a configurable idle/absolute lifetime, or set a Redis TTL on session entries and refresh on use. Reduce or invalidate the process-local `@@session_cache` on revocation events (e.g., pub/sub cache-bust) so `terminate`/`logout` take effect promptly across all workers. As hardening, compare the service password with a constant-time comparison (`Rack::Utils.secure_compare` / `OpenSSL.fixed_length_secure_compare`).
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-8dff895486f54851bdc4d16c5e1edaf8 (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Glob-metacharacter injection and unbounded recursive listing in volume file listing (Dir[])
findings.description:
##### Overview

The `_VOLUME` branch of `files` builds a shell-style glob directly from a user-supplied path: `Dir["/#{root}/#{path}/*"]`. `sanitize_path` strips `..`, control characters and a handful of punctuation, but it deliberately keeps `/` and does NOT strip glob metacharacters (`*`, `?`, `[`, `]`, `{`, `}`). An authenticated `system` user can therefore inject glob operators to enumerate the entire volume recursively (e.g. `path=**` yields `Dir["/root/**/*"]`) rather than just one directory level, and can force expensive/near-unbounded directory walks against large host volumes.

##### Attack Path

```
attacker (system perm) --params[:path]="**"--> sanitize_path keeps '*' --> Dir["/root/**/*"] --> recursive walk of whole volume --> deep file enumeration + CPU/memory load
```

`sanitize_path` (storage_controller.rb:604-616) only raises when the string changes; glob characters are not in its `tr`/`gsub` set, so they pass through unchanged and are interpolated straight into the `Dir[...]` glob at line 244. `**` triggers Ruby's recursive directory match, exposing the full volume tree (beyond the single level the UI intends) and, on a large mounted volume, materializing a very large result array in one request. Traversal outside the volume root is still prevented (`..` is rejected), so impact is limited to information disclosure within the volume plus an authenticated resource-consumption vector.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker is authenticated with `system` permission (the guard on `files`).
- At least one `OPENC3_*_VOLUME` is configured and mounted.
- Enterprise or Core; the glob expansion itself is not scope-gated for volumes.
findings.recommendation: Escape or reject glob metacharacters before building the Dir glob (e.g. use Dir.glob(File.join(root, path, '*'), File::FNM_... with escaping, or Dir.children on a validated directory), and/or bound the number of returned entries. Do not interpolate user input into a Dir[...] glob pattern.
findings.note: Glob injection / unbounded recursive listing via Dir[...] in storage_controller, using a user-supplied pattern. Authenticated 'system' user can enumerate files within the volume and cause expensive recursive listings (DoS). Exploitability moderate; impact medium. Fix: escape globs / bound depth. new/unverified.

findings.title: OTP one-time-use can be replayed via stale per-process session cache
findings.description:
##### Overview
One-time tokens issued by `/openc3-api/auth/otp` (`otp_`-prefixed) are consumed by `terminate_otp` inside `verify_no_service`, which deletes them from Redis and from the calling process's class-level `@@session_cache`. But that cache is per-process and refreshed only every ~5s (`SESSION_CACHE_TIMEOUT`). In a multi-worker/multi-replica deployment, a worker that cached the OTP before it was consumed on another worker will still serve it from its stale cache for up to the cache window, so the same OTP can authenticate twice. OTPs authenticate WebSocket subscriptions (permission `system`), so a replay grants a second unauthorized subscription.

##### Attack Path
```
OTP issued & stored in Redis --request A hits worker W1--> W1 fetches Redis, matches, terminate_otp deletes from Redis + W1 cache (OTP consumed)
  --request A' (same OTP) hits worker W2 within its ~5s cache window--> W2 still has OTP in stale @@session_cache --> match, returns true (replay)
  --> second WebSocket subscription authenticated with a supposedly one-time token
```
The class variable `@@session_cache` is not shared across processes; each worker independently caches `Store.hgetall(SESSIONS_KEY)` for up to `SESSION_CACHE_TIMEOUT` seconds. Deletion of a consumed OTP only updates the deleting worker's cache, so other workers can accept it until their cache refreshes. The same staleness also briefly keeps logged-out/terminated sessions valid.

##### Preconditions
- Deployment runs more than one API worker process/replica (typical for Puma clusters / scaled containers).
- Attacker possesses a valid OTP and can issue two near-simultaneous requests (<~5s apart) that land on different workers (or has a way to influence worker routing).
findings.recommendation: Make OTP consumption atomic and cross-process: delete-and-check the OTP directly against Redis (e.g. an atomic HDEL whose return value proves this caller consumed it) rather than trusting the per-process cache for OTP validation. Bypass the local cache for `otp_`-prefixed tokens.
findings.note: OTP replay via stale per-process cache. auth_controller can accept a one-time token twice across worker processes because revocation relies on a per-process cache with delayed cross-process propagation. Requires winning a small race across workers and possessing a valid OTP -> exploitability difficult; impact medium. Fix: atomic single-use consumption in the shared store. new/unverified.

findings.title: Outbound HTTP client follows redirects with no SSRF egress restrictions
findings.description:
##### Overview

`HttpClientInterface#connect` builds a Faraday connection with the `follow_redirects` middleware and the `net_http` adapter, with no restriction on redirect targets and no egress allowlist. The base host/port come from the interface configuration and the request path from the `HTTP_PATH` command item. Because 3xx redirects are followed automatically, a malicious or compromised upstream server (or an on-path/MITM attacker) can return a `Location` header pointing at internal addresses — e.g. the cloud metadata endpoint `169.254.169.254` or cluster-internal services — and the COSMOS server will follow it, turning a benign-looking outbound request into SSRF against the deployment's internal network, with the response body surfaced back through the interface. There is no host allowlist, no block of private/loopback/link-local ranges, and no redirect-count cap shown here. This is an SSRF amplifier rather than a primary SSRF: the connection target itself is operator-configured, so exploitation requires the configured upstream to be attacker-influenced or compromised.

##### Attack Path

```
operator configures HttpClientInterface(host) --> COSMOS requests host/path --> upstream returns 3xx Location: http://169.254.169.254/... --> Faraday follow_redirects follows automatically --> COSMOS fetches internal/metadata endpoint --> response returned as telemetry
```

The `follow_redirects` middleware transparently follows `Location` headers from the remote server. The remote server is only as trustworthy as the configured endpoint; if it is attacker-controlled, compromised, or reachable via MITM, it can redirect the client to internal resources the operator never intended to reach, and the body is returned back through the interface's response queue.

##### Preconditions

- An `HttpClientInterface` is configured (requires authenticated/system-level config; in Core, any authenticated user).
- The configured upstream is attacker-controlled, compromised, or MITM-able; OR the deployment runs in a cloud with a reachable metadata endpoint / internal services.
- Deployment lacks independent network egress controls that would block internal access.
findings.recommendation: Disable automatic redirect following, or constrain it: cap the redirect count and re-validate each redirect target against a host allowlist while denying private (RFC1918), loopback, and link-local (169.254.0.0/16) ranges before following. Additionally enforce SSRF egress controls at the network layer (block the metadata endpoint and internal CIDRs) so a compromised upstream cannot pivot into the cluster.
findings.note: Redirect-following SSRF amplifier. http_client_interface follows redirects, which can amplify requests to attacker-chosen locations, but requires an attacker-controlled or compromised upstream endpoint first. Exploitability difficult; impact medium. Fix: bound/validate redirects. new/unverified.

findings.title: Path traversal / arbitrary file write via unsanitized uploaded gem filename
findings.description:
##### Overview

In `PluginsController#create`, when a plugin is uploaded directly (the `params[:plugin]` branch), the destination path is built as `temp_dir + '/' + original_filename` where `original_filename = file.original_filename` — the client-supplied multipart filename, which Rails does not sanitize. A filename containing `../` sequences causes `FileUtils.cp` to write the uploaded bytes outside the freshly-created `Dir.mktmpdir` directory (arbitrary file write). Notably the store-provided sibling path uses `File.basename(store_version['gem_filename'])` (line 145), so the base name is stripped there — the direct-upload path is the one inconsistent branch that omits that protection. The action is guarded by `authorization('admin')`, and an admin can already achieve code execution through the intended plugin-install flow (`install_phase1` unpacks and loads the gem), so this traversal grants no privilege beyond what the admin already has; hence LOW severity. It is reported because it is a genuine missing-sanitization gap and a parallel-structure inconsistency with the store branch.

##### Attack Path

```
admin multipart upload with filename="../../openc3/target.rb" --> params[:plugin].original_filename (unsanitized) --> gem_file_path = temp_dir + '/' + original_filename --> FileUtils.cp writes attacker bytes to path outside temp_dir --> arbitrary file write
```

The uploaded file's `original_filename` is taken verbatim (line 152) and concatenated onto `temp_dir` (line 158). Because `../` is not stripped (unlike the `File.basename` used on line 145 for the store branch), `FileUtils.cp` (line 159) resolves the destination outside the temp directory, allowing an authenticated admin to write the uploaded contents to an arbitrary filesystem location the API process can write to.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker holds an `admin`-authorized token/session (enforced at line 110).
- The attacker uses the direct-upload branch (`params[:plugin]`, no `store_plugin_id`), so `File.basename` on line 145 is not applied.
- Because admin already has code-execution capability via legitimate plugin installation, exploitation yields no additional privilege — impact is bounded to the admin trust level.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize the upload filename before building the path, e.g. `original_filename = File.basename(file.original_filename)` (matching the store branch), or route it through `sanitize_params` / an allowlist. Also validate that `gem_file_path` resolves inside `temp_dir` before `FileUtils.cp`.
findings.note: Admin-only upload filename path traversal -> arbitrary file write to the plugins directory. Gated by admin, who already has plugin-install code-execution capability, so no privilege gain. Exploitability difficult (admin); impact low. Fix: sanitize/basename the upload filename. new/unverified (resembles path-traversal advisory GHSA-4jvx-93h3-f45h, which is outside this profile's cited advisory set).

findings.title: Pre-authentication JSON deserialization with create_additions:true on the JSON-RPC endpoint
findings.description:
##### Overview

The unauthenticated JSON-RPC endpoint (`/openc3-api/api`) parses the raw request body with `JSON.parse(request_data, allow_nan: true, create_additions: true)` inside `JsonRpcRequest.from_json`, before any authentication and before the method whitelist is consulted. `create_additions: true` tells the parser to instantiate a Ruby object for any nested `{"json_class":"<Name>", ...}` element by calling `<Name>.json_create(hash)`. This is the classic Ruby unsafe-deserialization / object-injection pattern, and the class name is fully attacker-controlled from the request body. In the code as shipped the only classes that expose `json_create` are `String` (via `require 'json/add/string'`) and a custom, benign `Float` defined in this file, so no dangerous gadget is currently reachable and I could not demonstrate a concrete impact. The endpoint's safety therefore rests entirely on the implicit, undocumented invariant that no class defining a dangerous `json_create` is ever loaded into the cmd-tlm-api process. That invariant is fragile: a single future `require 'json/add/core'` (present in this project's own git history), or any gem/monkey-patch that defines `json_create`, would silently convert this unauthenticated path into a real object-injection primitive.

##### Attack Path

```
anonymous HTTP POST /openc3-api/api (JSON body)
  --> ApiController#api (no authenticating before_action)
  --> handle_post --> JsonDRb#process_request
  --> JsonRpcRequest.from_json(body, headers)
  --> JSON.parse(body, allow_nan: true, create_additions: true)   [before whitelist/authorize]
  --> <json_class>.json_create(attacker-controlled hash)  for every loaded gadget class
  --> object injection (today limited to String/Float => benign; dangerous gadget => up to RCE)
```

The parse executes at `json_rpc.rb:283`, which is reached from `json_drb.rb:252` (`JsonRpcRequest.from_json`) *before* the whitelist test at `json_drb.rb:257` and before the per-method `authorize()` that lives inside each whitelisted API method. The HTTP entry point `ApiController#api` has no authenticating `before_action`; `AuthError`/`ForbiddenError` are only rescued *after* `handle_post` returns, proving authentication happens strictly downstream of the parse. `create_additions` dispatch happens during parsing of any nested value, so it fires even though `from_json` later validates `jsonrpc`/`method`/`id` (and even if that validation ultimately raises). Consequently the deserializer processes fully attacker-controlled bytes with zero authentication. Today the reachable `json_create` set is String + Float only, so the concrete outcome is limited to constructing ordinary String/Float objects; the severity is driven up to CRITICAL the moment a dangerous `json_create` gadget is present in the load set.

##### Preconditions

- Network reachability to the cmd-tlm-api `/openc3-api/api` endpoint (routed through Traefik in a default COSMOS deployment). No authentication token is required to reach the parser.
- For any impact beyond benign String/Float construction: a class exposing a dangerous `json_create` must be loaded into the cmd-tlm-api Ruby process (e.g. `json/add/core`, which defines `json_create` for Symbol/Struct/Regexp/etc., or any dependency/monkey-patch defining `json_create`). No such gadget exists in the repository at commit 77acb91. This is the portion I could not fully verify, because the complete transitive `require` graph of the installed gem bundle is not present in the source tree.
findings.recommendation: Parse the RPC request without global object reconstruction: use `JSON.parse(request_data, allow_nan: true)` (create_additions defaults to false) and handle the protocol's only custom types (String byte-arrays and non-finite Floats) explicitly after parsing, rather than relying on global `json_create` dispatch. If create_additions must be retained, gate it behind an explicit allowlist of expected `json_class` values (e.g. only `String`/`Float`) and reject any others. Where feasible, authenticate the request before deserializing the body.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-912d80caa1e749dea0b1111e0efbb4e9 (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Ruby stack traces returned to authenticated clients in error responses
findings.description:
##### Overview

Each generic `rescue StandardError` handler in `TriggerGroupController` serializes the exception's full `backtrace` into the JSON 500 response body. An authenticated user who induces an unexpected error receives absolute server file paths, gem paths, and line numbers, disclosing internal implementation details (CWE-209). The endpoints require authentication and no secrets are leaked directly, so impact is limited to reconnaissance value.

##### Attack Path

```
authenticated user (system / script_run role)
  --sends request that triggers backend/validation error--> TriggerGroup action
  --raises non-domain StandardError--> rescue StandardError
  --renders--> { status:'error', message:..., type:..., backtrace: e.backtrace } (HTTP 500)
  --leads to--> disclosure of server file paths, gem versions, and code structure
```

Actions gate on `authorization('system')` (index/show) or `authorization('script_run')` (create/destroy), so a caller must be authenticated. When an exception falls outside the handled `TriggerGroupInputError`/`TriggerGroupError` types (e.g. a Redis/deploy error), the generic rescue returns `e.backtrace`. In Enterprise these are lower-privilege roles, making the disclosure meaningful.

##### Preconditions

- Authenticated `system` or `script_run` user; the leak matters most under Enterprise role separation.
- Ability to induce a non-domain `StandardError` (e.g. a backend/`deploy` failure or store error).
findings.recommendation: Remove `e.backtrace` (and ideally `type`) from client responses. Log full detail server-side via `log_error(e)` and return only a generic message and status code; gate any verbose diagnostics behind an explicit debug/env flag.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-2e0d29156d5249bbb8f974cec1a027cd (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Ruby stack traces returned to authenticated clients in error responses
findings.description:
##### Overview

Every generic `rescue StandardError` handler in `TriggerController` serializes the exception's full `backtrace` into the JSON 500 response body. An authenticated user who induces an unexpected error receives absolute server file paths, gem paths, and line numbers, disclosing internal implementation details (CWE-209) useful for reconnaissance and matching gem versions to known CVEs. No secrets are leaked directly, and the endpoints require authentication, so impact is limited.

##### Attack Path

```
authenticated user (system / script_run role)
  --sends crafted/malformed request--> Trigger action (e.g. create/update)
  --raises non-domain StandardError--> rescue StandardError
  --renders--> { status:'error', message:..., type:..., backtrace: e.backtrace } (HTTP 500)
  --leads to--> disclosure of server file paths, gem versions, and code structure
```

Each action first calls `authorization('system')` (reads) or `authorization('script_run')` (mutations), so the caller must be authenticated. `create`/`update` accept attacker-influenced JSON (`left: {}`, `right: {}`, `operator`, etc.) that can raise exceptions outside the handled domain types, falling through to the generic rescue which returns `e.backtrace`. In Enterprise these roles are lower-privilege, making the leak to such a principal meaningful; in Core the authenticated principal is the shared-password holder.

##### Preconditions

- Authenticated `system` (reads) or `script_run` (mutations) user; the info leak is most relevant in Enterprise where those are non-admin roles.
- Ability to induce a non-domain `StandardError` (e.g. malformed nested `left`/`right` payload, or a backend/Redis error).
findings.recommendation: Remove `e.backtrace` (and ideally `type`) from client responses. Log full exception detail server-side via `log_error(e)` and return only a generic message plus the status code. If verbose diagnostics are needed, gate them behind an explicit debug/env flag (e.g. `OPENC3_FULL_BACKTRACE`).
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-2e0d29156d5249bbb8f974cec1a027cd (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Server backtraces disclosed in API error responses
findings.description:
##### Overview

Every `rescue` block in `QueuesController` renders the exception's full `backtrace` (and class name) directly in the JSON error response (`render json: { status: 'error', message: e.message, type: e.class.to_s, backtrace: e.backtrace }`). This leaks server-side file paths, gem/library versions, and internal call structure to any client able to trigger an error. The endpoints require `cmd_info`/`cmd` authorization, so this is exposure to authenticated users rather than the anonymous internet, which keeps it LOW; it is nonetheless a real information-disclosure defense gap and aids reconnaissance for further attacks. The same pattern appears in sibling controllers (e.g. `reaction_controller.rb`).

##### Attack Path

```
authenticated request that triggers an exception (e.g. malformed params) --> rescue StandardError => e --> render json includes e.backtrace --> client receives server file paths + internal structure
```

Any handled error path returns the raw backtrace array to the caller. An authenticated user can deliberately provoke errors to enumerate absolute server paths, gem versions, and internal code organization, which is useful reconnaissance for chaining other vulnerabilities.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker holds a token with `cmd_info` (reads) or `cmd` (mutations) permission — i.e. an authenticated, non-anonymous user.
- Attacker can induce an exception in one of the actions (commonly trivial via malformed input).
- No cross-tenant or privilege boundary is crossed; the leak is limited to server implementation details.
findings.recommendation: Do not return `e.backtrace` in API responses. Log the backtrace server-side and return only a generic error message (optionally a correlation id). Apply the same change to the other controllers that echo backtraces.
findings.note: Backtrace/internal-error disclosure to authenticated clients (root cause across controllers). Generic rescues return e.backtrace/e.message in the HTTP response, leaking server paths and internals that aid recon. Same pattern confirmed in queues_controller, notes_controller, trigger_controller, trigger_group_controller (and noted in sibling controllers e.g. reaction_controller). Exploitability moderate (authenticated, trigger an error); impact medium (info disclosure). Fix: return generic error, log details server-side. Canonical for the backtrace-disclosure root cause; duplicates sfind-faf79932bda14e84a17ad467f1b94c55, sfind-556776be064c4fd7b62e6edd07addbc0, sfind-efcccb3305644d4288bb221deb09edab dismissed. new/unverified.

findings.title: Service password compared with non-constant-time string equality
findings.description:
##### Overview
`AuthModel.verify` compares the presented token against the `OPENC3_SERVICE_PASSWORD` environment secret using Ruby's `==` operator, which is not constant-time. This comparison executes on every authorized API request (the core authorization path calls `AuthModel.verify(token)`) and on the `/auth/verify_service` endpoint, giving a remote party a comparison oracle against the service secret. It is a defense-in-depth / secret-handling weakness rather than a practically exploitable remote attack.

##### Attack Path
```
attacker-supplied token (Authorization header or /auth/verify_service body) --> AuthModel.verify --> service_password == token (variable-time) --> timing signal correlated with matching prefix
```
Ruby `String#==` short-circuits on length mismatch and otherwise performs a byte compare that can return early, so its execution time can correlate with how much of the secret matches. In theory this leaks information about the service password; in practice, network jitter and the small size of the timing delta make remote exploitation very difficult, which is why this is rated LOW.

##### Preconditions
- `OPENC3_SERVICE_PASSWORD` is configured (the service-password feature is in use).
- Attacker can send many requests and measure response timing precisely enough to overcome network noise (generally impractical over a real network).
findings.recommendation: Use a constant-time comparison for the secret, e.g. Rack::Utils.secure_compare or OpenSSL.fixed_length_secure_compare (after equalizing/hashing lengths), instead of ==. Longer term, replace the static shared service password with short-lived service tokens as the in-code TODO notes.
findings.note: Non-constant-time comparison of the service/password value in auth_model, a timing side-channel. Impractical to exploit remotely over network jitter. Exploitability difficult; impact low. Fix: use a constant-time compare. Canonical for the timing root cause; duplicate sfind-8bc496501e9c40edbd8e9ba293eae21e dismissed. new/unverified.

findings.title: Service password compared with non-constant-time string equality
findings.description:
##### Overview
The service-password check in `AuthModel.verify` (reached unauthenticated via `POST /openc3-api/auth/verify_service`) compares the caller-supplied token to `ENV['OPENC3_SERVICE_PASSWORD']` using Ruby's `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is not constant-time. In principle this leaks a timing side-channel about how many leading bytes of the service password are correct. In practice, remote timing attacks against a single `String#==` over the network are extremely difficult due to jitter, so real-world exploitability is low, but the matcher guidance calls for reviewing token comparisons for timing issues and the correct fix is cheap.

##### Attack Path
```
unauthenticated POST /auth/verify_service (guessed password) --service_password == token--> response time varies with match-prefix length --statistical timing analysis--> recover service password byte-by-byte
```
Unlike the user password (Argon2 verify) and session tokens (hash lookup), the service password uses a plain `==`. A valid service password yields a full session token, so recovering it grants authenticated access. The verify_service endpoint is rate-limited (shared counter) which further constrains any timing measurement, reinforcing the low severity.

##### Preconditions
- `OPENC3_SERVICE_PASSWORD` is configured (service-password path enabled).
- Attacker can make many timed requests to `/auth/verify_service` and statistically distinguish sub-microsecond comparison differences over the network (impractical in most deployments).
findings.recommendation: Use a constant-time comparison for the service password, e.g. `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare` / `Rack::Utils.secure_compare` (guarding for length), instead of `==`.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-cdaf6f74915b46169d0aeb8e22be24e2 (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Session and OTP tokens never expire (stored timestamp never enforced)
findings.description:
##### Overview
`generate_session` stores each session/OTP token in the `OPENC3__SESSIONS` Redis hash with a creation timestamp as the value, but `verify_no_service` treats any token present in the hash as valid and never consults that timestamp. There is no idle or absolute session timeout: a session token remains valid indefinitely until an explicit `logout` (which happens on password change) or `terminate`. A non-consumed OTP token likewise never times out. A leaked/stolen session token therefore grants access for an unbounded period.

##### Attack Path
```
generate_session stores token->iso8601 timestamp --> verify_no_service returns true purely on hash membership (timestamp ignored) --> stolen token remains valid forever until logout/terminate
```
The issuance path records `Time.now.iso8601` as the hash value, implying an intended expiry, but the verification path only checks `@@session_cache[token]` / `Store.hgetall` membership and never compares the stored time against a max age. Consequently the token lifetime is effectively infinite.

##### Preconditions
- Attacker obtains a valid session token (e.g. via logging, browser storage theft, proxy capture, or shared-terminal reuse).
- The legitimate user does not change the password (password change calls logout and clears all sessions).
findings.recommendation: Enforce a session lifetime: record issuance time (already stored) and reject tokens older than a configurable absolute/idle timeout in verify_no_service, and/or set a TTL and periodically prune expired entries. Apply a short expiry to OTP tokens as well.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-8dff895486f54851bdc4d16c5e1edaf8 (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Session and OTP tokens never expire; cross-process revocation delayed up to 5 minutes
findings.description:
##### Overview

`generate_session` stores each session/OTP token in the `OPENC3__SESSIONS` Redis hash with a creation timestamp, but `verify_no_service` only checks hash membership and never compares that timestamp against a TTL, and no code prunes old entries. Session tokens — and any generated-but-unused OTP tokens — therefore stay valid indefinitely until an explicit `logout`/password change. Additionally, `verify_no_service` serves tokens from a per-process class-variable cache for up to `SESSION_CACHE_TIMEOUT` (5 minutes), so a token revoked in one worker is still accepted by other worker processes for up to 5 minutes. This is a defense-in-depth weakness that amplifies the impact of any token leak and slows revocation.

##### Attack Path

```
token minted (generate_session) --stored with timestamp but no TTL--> OPENC3__SESSIONS
  --> verify_no_service checks presence only (no expiry check) --> token valid until password change
  --> revocation: logout in process A --> process B still accepts token from @@session_cache for up to 5 min
```

The stored `Time.now.iso8601` value is never read back, and there is no idle or absolute timeout. A token captured from logs, browser history, a proxy, or an OTP placed in a URL remains usable until someone changes the password. The 5-minute per-process session cache further delays propagation of `terminate`/`logout`, so revoking a session is not immediate cluster-wide.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker obtains a valid session or unused OTP token (e.g. via log/referrer/proxy leakage, shoulder-surfing, or a separate disclosure bug). Not directly exploitable by an unauthenticated attacker on its own; it increases the blast radius and lifetime of any leaked token and delays revocation across processes.
findings.recommendation: Persist an expiry with each session and enforce idle/absolute timeouts in verify_no_service (compare the stored timestamp, or set a per-field/hash TTL), and prune expired entries. Give OTP tokens a short absolute expiry independent of use. On logout/terminate, invalidate the per-process cache promptly (e.g. via a pub/sub invalidation) so revocation propagates without a 5-minute delay.
findings.note: Session/OTP tokens never expire and revocation is delayed. auth_model stores session tokens with no TTL/issue-time check and relies on a ~5-minute per-process cache, so a leaked token stays valid indefinitely and revocation lags across workers. No standalone exploit -> amplifies any token leak. Exploitability difficult (needs a leaked token); impact medium. Fix: token TTL + prompt revocation. Canonical for the session-expiry root cause; duplicates sfind-8b02b929aecb455ab573424275021743, sfind-8fce2b4c3f27456eba771442f6d59f03, sfind-a573684eb0da47fbba95768ebea2f9a6 dismissed. new/unverified.

findings.title: Session tokens never expire (stored issue timestamp is never enforced)
findings.description:
##### Overview
`generate_session` mints an opaque `SecureRandom` token and stores it in the `OPENC3__SESSIONS` Redis hash with the value set to the ISO-8601 issue time, but nothing ever reads that timestamp to expire the token, and no Redis TTL is applied to the hash or its fields. `verify_no_service` accepts a token purely on existence (`@@session_cache[token]` / `Store.hgetall`), so a session token remains valid indefinitely until the password is changed (which calls `logout` and wipes ALL sessions). There is no idle timeout and no absolute lifetime, so a leaked/captured session token grants access forever.

##### Attack Path
```
operator logs in --> generate_session stores token with issue-time value (never read)
  --token leaks (proxy log, browser history, backup, shoulder-surf)--> attacker replays token
  --verify_no_service checks existence only, no expiry--> access granted indefinitely
```
The stored `Time.now.iso8601` value signals clear intent to expire sessions, but no code path compares it against the current time or sets a TTL. The only invalidation events are `terminate` (single token, used for OTP consumption) and `logout` (all tokens, only on password change). So an attacker who obtains a token once retains access until an operator happens to rotate the password.

##### Preconditions
- Attacker obtains a valid session token via some out-of-band leak (this finding is the missing-control that turns a token leak into permanent access; it is not independently exploitable without a token).
- The password is not rotated (rotation is the only event that invalidates existing sessions).
findings.recommendation: Enforce session lifetime: either set a Redis TTL on session entries at issuance (and refresh on use for idle timeout), or compare the stored issue timestamp against a configurable max age in verify_no_service and treat expired tokens as invalid (deleting them). Keep the existing logout-on-password-change behavior.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-8dff895486f54851bdc4d16c5e1edaf8 (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: Session/authorization token logged in cleartext (API headers at debug, body at info)
findings.description:
##### Overview

`ApiController#api` builds `request_headers` from every `HTTP_*` env entry — which includes `HTTP_AUTHORIZATION`, i.e. the caller's session token or password — and logs the entire header hash via `OpenC3::Logger.debug("API headers: #{request_headers}")`. It also logs the full request body at info level. If debug logging is enabled, valid bearer credentials are written to the log stream in cleartext (CWE-532), where anyone with log access can harvest and replay them. Because Core session tokens do not expire (see the connection.rb finding), a token captured from logs remains usable indefinitely.

##### Attack Path

```
client sends Authorization: <session token> --> ApiController#api collects HTTP_* headers (api_controller.rb:30)
  --> Logger.debug("API headers: ...") writes token to logs (api_controller.rb:39)
  --> operator/attacker with log read access harvests token --> replays as valid session
```

The token is transported in the `Authorization` header, which is captured into `request_headers` on line 30 and emitted on line 39. This is an information-disclosure / secret-in-log issue rather than a direct external RCE; its impact depends on who can read the service logs and whether debug level is enabled in the deployment.

##### Preconditions

- Debug log level enabled for the token exposure (the body-at-info log on line 38 does not normally contain the token, since the token rides in the header).
- An actor able to read the cmd-tlm-api log output (log aggregation system, container logs, or a co-located account).
findings.recommendation: Redact or omit sensitive headers (Authorization, and any cookie/manual-token headers) before logging. Log a fixed allowlist of non-sensitive headers, or replace the token value with a fingerprint/`[REDACTED]`. Avoid logging full request bodies that may contain credentials.
findings.note: Authorization/session token logged in cleartext at debug level in api_controller. Requires debug logging enabled plus access to logs -> exploitability difficult; impact medium (credential exposure). Fix: redact the token before logging. Secret value not reproduced here [REDACTED]. new/unverified.

findings.title: Unauthenticated access to plugin store listing endpoint
findings.description:
##### Overview

`PluginStoreController#index` renders `OpenC3::PluginStoreModel.all()` with no `authorization(...)` call, unlike the generic `ModelController`/`PluginsController` actions which require `system`/`admin`. Any client that can reach the Rails cmd-tlm-api can read the cached plugin-store catalog and, on first access when the cache is empty, trigger the `ensure_exists` before_action which performs an outbound HTTP fetch to the configured `store_url`. Impact is limited: the catalog is non-sensitive marketplace data and the outbound URL is not attacker-controlled (it defaults to a hardcoded store and is otherwise admin-set via the `store_url` DEFAULT setting), so this is primarily a missing-control / defense-in-depth gap rather than a data breach or SSRF.

##### Attack Path

```
unauthenticated HTTP GET /pluginstore --> PluginStoreController#index (no authorization) --> before_action ensure_exists --> PluginStoreModel.ensure_exists --> (if cache empty) PluginStoreModel.update --> Faraday.get(store_url) --> render catalog JSON
```

The `index` action has no authorization guard, so an anonymous request returns the plugin-store catalog. The `ensure_exists` before_action calls `PluginStoreModel.update` only when the cache is empty/errored; that update issues an outbound Faraday GET to `store_url`. Because `store_url` is server/admin configuration (default is a fixed OpenC3 store URL), an unauthenticated caller cannot direct the request to an internal target, so the outbound fetch is not a usable SSRF primitive — the real issue is simply the absence of authentication on the endpoint.

##### Preconditions

- Network reachability to the `openc3-cosmos-cmd-tlm-api` service (in a standard deployment this sits behind Traefik and requires no credentials for this route).
- To cause the outbound fetch, the plugin-store cache must be empty or in an error state (e.g. first access after startup); steady-state requests only read the cache.
- No control over `store_url` is available to the unauthenticated caller, so no internal-target SSRF is possible via this path.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit `return unless authorization('system')` (or the appropriate read permission) at the start of `index`, matching the other model-backed controllers. If the endpoint is intended to be public (mirroring `NewsController#index`), document that intent and ensure `ensure_exists` cannot be used to trigger repeated outbound fetches by unauthenticated callers.
findings.note: Unauthenticated plugin-store catalog listing (plugin_store_controller). The outbound URL is admin-controlled/default, not attacker-controlled, and the listed data is non-sensitive. Exploitability trivial; impact low. new/unverified.

findings.title: Unauthenticated scope enumeration via GET /scopes
findings.description:
##### Overview
`ScopesController#index` explicitly performs no authorization (`# No authorization required`) and returns the full list of configured scope names to any caller, including fully unauthenticated ones. This exposes the tenant/scope namespace of the deployment. It appears intentional (the login/scope-selector UI needs the scope list before authentication, matching upstream OpenC3), so this is a low-severity information-disclosure / defense-in-depth gap rather than a clear defect. The `create` and `destroy` actions in the same controller are correctly guarded by `superadmin`, and `destroy` spawns the CLI via array-form `ChildProcess.build` (no shell), so `params[:id]` cannot be used for command injection.

##### Attack Path
```
GET /scopes (no token) --> ScopesController#index (no authorization guard) --> ScopeModel.names() --> JSON list of all scope names returned to anonymous caller
```
Unlike `ModelController#index` (which requires the `system` permission), this subclass overrides `index` with no guard, so the response is served to unauthenticated requests. `ScopeModel.names` returns only the scope name strings (`store.hkeys(...).sort`), so no secret material is leaked—only the set of scope identifiers.

##### Preconditions
- Network reachability to the cmd-tlm-api `/scopes` endpoint.
- No authentication required.
- Low sensitivity: only scope names are disclosed; appears to be intended behavior for the pre-login scope selector.
findings.recommendation: If the pre-login scope list is genuinely required by the UI, keep it but consider limiting exposure (e.g. only when auth is not yet configured) or documenting it as intentional. Otherwise add `return unless authorization('system')` to match the base ModelController#index.
findings.note: Unauthenticated scope enumeration (scopes_controller index). Likely intentional pre-login behavior; leaks scope names. Exploitability trivial; impact low (defense-in-depth). new/unverified.

findings.title: Unauthenticated version/edition disclosure via /openc3-api/info
findings.description:
##### Overview

The Core `InfoController#info` action renders `{ version: OPENC3_VERSION, license: 'OpenC3', enterprise: false }` with no authorization guard. Any unauthenticated remote client can read the exact COSMOS version and edition. This is a minor information-disclosure / fingerprinting aid (helps an attacker match the deployment to known-version CVEs). It is almost certainly intentional — the login UI queries `/info` before authentication to decide whether to show Core vs Enterprise flows — so impact is limited to version/edition disclosure only (no secrets or user data).

##### Attack Path

```
anonymous HTTP GET /openc3-api/info --route--> InfoController#info (no authorization() call) --> exact version + edition returned to unauthenticated caller
```

The route `get "/info" => "info#info"` lives under the `openc3-api` scope and is forwarded by Traefik's `PathPrefix('/openc3-api')` router. The action returns constants immediately without calling `authorization`, so the version and edition are always readable pre-auth.

##### Preconditions

- Network reachability to the COSMOS Traefik entrypoint (anyone who can reach the login page).
- No credentials required; the endpoint is unauthenticated by design to support the pre-login UI.
findings.recommendation: If exact version disclosure to anonymous users is not required, gate the endpoint (or return a coarse/no version field pre-auth). If the pre-login UI genuinely needs the edition flag, return only `enterprise: false` without the precise `OPENC3_VERSION`. Otherwise document this as an accepted, low-risk disclosure.
findings.note: Unauthenticated version/edition disclosure (info_controller). Likely intentional for the pre-login UI, but aids version-based recon. Exploitability trivial; impact low (defense-in-depth). new/unverified.

findings.title: Unhandled exceptions return full stack backtrace to the client (information disclosure)
findings.description:
##### Overview
The `action` rescue helper in `NotesController` catches any `StandardError` raised inside an action body and renders the exception's full, unfiltered backtrace back to the HTTP client in the JSON response body (`backtrace: e.backtrace`). An authenticated caller who can trigger an unexpected error obtains absolute server filesystem paths, gem names/versions, and internal call structure — useful reconnaissance for further attacks. This is an information-disclosure / defense-in-depth weakness, not a direct compromise.

##### Attack Path
```
GET /openc3-api/notes?scope=DEFAULT&start=<valid>&stop=<valid>&limit=abc
  --> NoteModel.range(..., limit: "abc")
  --> Store.zrangebyscore(... LIMIT 0 abc) --Redis::CommandError--> rescue StandardError
  --> render json: { ..., backtrace: e.backtrace } --leaks--> absolute paths / internals
```
The `index` action permits `:limit` and forwards it verbatim via `**hash.symbolize_keys` into `SortedModel.range`, which passes it to `Store.zrangebyscore(pk, start, stop, limit: [0, limit])`. `Store` delegates unknown methods straight to the redis client (`store_autoload.rb` `method_missing`), so a non-integer `limit` produces a `Redis::CommandError` (a `StandardError`, not `ArgumentError`/`TypeError`/`SortedError`). That falls through to the generic `rescue StandardError => e` branch of `action`, which — unlike `log_error`, which filters the backtrace before logging — renders the raw `e.backtrace` array directly to the response. Any StandardError path (redis errors, unexpected nil, etc.) reaches this branch.

##### Preconditions
- Caller passes the `authorization('system')` guard on `index`/`show` (in COSMOS Core this is any holder of the configured password, or anyone at all when `$openc3_authorize` is unset; in Enterprise, any user with the lowest `system` role).
- Caller supplies input that raises a `StandardError` other than `ArgumentError`/`TypeError`/`SortedError` inside the action body (e.g. `limit` set to a non-integer string alongside valid `start`/`stop`).
- Same pattern is duplicated in `metadata_controller.rb` (out of this batch's primary scope but affected identically).
findings.recommendation: Do not return `e.backtrace` in the HTTP response. Remove the `backtrace` key from the `rescue StandardError` branch (log it server-side via `log_error(e)` only, as is already done). Return a generic error message to the client and reserve detailed backtraces for server logs, optionally gated behind `ENV['OPENC3_FULL_BACKTRACE']` for development only.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-2e0d29156d5249bbb8f974cec1a027cd (same root cause); merged there during aggregation.

findings.title: delete_modified wipes a target's modified config with only 'system' (view) permission
findings.description:
##### Overview

`TargetsController#delete_modified` deletes every object under `{scope}/targets_modified/{target}/` (via `OpenC3::TargetModel.delete_modified`), destroying all of a target's user modifications (custom screens, procedures, cmd/tlm overrides, lib files). It is guarded only by `authorization('system')` — the view-level permission — whereas the sibling full-target `destroy` inherited from `ModelController` requires `authorization('admin')`, and deletions of the same `targets_modified` objects via `StorageController` require `system_set`/`admin`. An Enterprise user with only `system` (view) permission in a scope can therefore irreversibly delete a target's modifications, an integrity/availability impact from a read-level role.

##### Attack Path

```
attacker (system/view perm in scope S) --DELETE modified files route (id=TARGET)--> authorization('system') passes --> TargetModel.delete_modified lists and delete_object's all {S}/targets_modified/TARGET/* --> target modifications destroyed
```

`delete_modified` (targets_controller.rb:47-59) only requires `system`, then calls `TargetModel.delete_modified` (target_model.rb:147-161) which enumerates and deletes every key under the target's `targets_modified` prefix. The convention elsewhere (ModelController#destroy uses `admin`; StorageController targets_modified deletes use `system_set`/`admin`) shows `system` is weaker than this destructive side effect.

##### Preconditions

- Enterprise deployment with real per-scope RBAC where a role can hold `system` without higher permissions (Core ignores permission strings).
- Attacker is authenticated with `system` permission in the scope (supplied as `params[:scope]`).
- Attacker knows a valid target `id` (target name) in that scope.
findings.recommendation: Require at least 'system_set' (preferably 'admin', to match ModelController#destroy and StorageController targets_modified deletes) on delete_modified. Keep the read-only actions (all_modified, modified_files, download) at 'system'.
findings.note: Destructive delete_modified guarded only by read-level 'system'. targets_controller#delete_modified lets a view-level Enterprise user delete a target's modified config/overlay. Exploitability moderate; impact medium (integrity/availability). Same weak-authorization theme as tables/storage findings but a distinct action. Fix: require a write/admin permission. new/unverified.
